And she who was the chief queen of King Araṇemin stood before the Blessed One.
Scattering powders of gośīrṣa sandalwood and uragasāra sandalwood over the Blessed One,
she took the radiant jewel that had belonged to King Araṇemin and placed it of her own accord before the Blessed One.
Then, by the light of that jewel-gem, that entire garden was constantly and perpetually suffused with a magnificent radiance;
and by the light of the Buddha, this entire great trichiliocosm world-system was constantly and perpetually suffused.
For each and every disciple, a footstool made of gośīrṣa sandalwood was set out;
and behind each disciple, an all-white elephant-king was stationed, upon which a wheel-treasure (*cakraratna*) of exactly the same form and human proportions was placed, just as for the Blessed One.
And before each disciple, a maiden adorned with every ornament was stationed, scattering powders of gośīrṣa and uragasāra sandalwood.
And before each individual disciple, a lapis lazuli gem was placed. Within the garden on all sides, various kinds of musical instruments were played;
outside the garden, the counselor-jewel moved about in every direction together with the fourfold army.
Then, noble son, King Araṇemi went out from the city day after day to see, pay homage to, and attend upon the Blessed One.
He traveled by vehicle as far as the ground would allow for a vehicle; then, alighting from the vehicle, he entered the park on foot.
Having entered, he approached the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha, and having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha Ratnagarbha.
Having circumambulated him three times,

he personally provided the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha with water for washing his hands, and himself served him with his own hands an abundant variety of excellent foods— both solid and soft, as well as those to be licked and drunk.

He satisfied and served them; having personally satisfied and served them, and knowing that the Blessed One had finished eating, with his hands washed and his bowl removed, he himself took a fan and fanned the Blessed One.
And for each disciple, a thousand princes and a thousand local kings performed such service, taking fans and fanning the disciples.
Immediately upon the conclusion of the distribution of food, many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of living beings entered the grove to hear the Dharma.
In the sky, many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of gods rained down a shower of flowers, played divine musical instruments,
and suspended celestial parasols, garments, and ornaments.
And there were four million yakṣas dressed in blue garments who brought logs of *gośīrṣa* sandalwood from Candanadvīpa;
they prepared food for the sake of the Blessed One and the community of monks.
During the night, King Araṇemin himself lit many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of lamps before the Blessed One and the community of monks.
Then, noble son, King Araṇemi stood before the Blessed One, placing a single lamp-stand upon his head, two upon his shoulders, two upon his hands, and two upon his feet;
throughout all the nights he kept lamps burning before the Blessed One,
and by the power of the Blessed One, his body remained untiring.
He experienced such bodily bliss as that of a monk who has attained the third dhyāna; thus, with body untiring and mind untiring, he attended upon the Blessed One for three months.
Likewise, a thousand princes, eighty-four thousand minor kings, and hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of other living beings [did the same].

Each individual attendant served every single disciple for three months with royal provisions and such services as the King Araṇemin had provided for the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha; likewise, the chief queen served them for three months with perfumes and flowers.
In the same way, many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of other maidens served each disciple for three months with flowers and perfumes.
Then, noble son, at the end of three months, King Araṇemin offered eighty-four thousand *niṣka* coins made of Jāmbūnada gold to the Blessed One.

He also offered eighty-four thousand golden wheel-treasures (*cakraratna*), preceded by the wheel-treasure, to the Blessed One. Furthermore, he offered eighty-four thousand elephants, all white in color, preceded by the elephant-treasure (*hastiratna*), to the Blessed One.

He presented to the Blessed One eighty-four thousand horses, preceded by the horse-treasure; he presented to the Blessed One eighty-four thousand sun-crystal jewels, preceded by the jewel-treasure; [and] eighty-four thousand householder-treasures, preceded by the householder-treasure. (KpSū 60)
He offered eighty-four thousand princes to the Blessed One for his service.

He offered eighty-four thousand minor kings, led by the Jewel of the Commander-in-Chief, to the Blessed One for his service. And he offered eighty-four thousand cities, led by the city of Añcuna, as sources of sustenance for the Blessed One and the community of monks.
Eighty-four thousand wish-fulfilling trees made of jewels; eighty-four thousand heaps of flowers made of jewels; eighty-four thousand parasols made of the seven precious gems;

eighty-four thousand sets of magnificent royal garments worthy of kings; eighty-four thousand garlands made of jewels; and ornaments, pedestals, head-jewels, earrings, golden threads, pearl necklaces, sandals, couches, footstools, vessels, drums, conchs, bells, and banners.
She presented to the Blessed One golden water-pitchers and lamp-stands;
she presented to the Blessed One birds made of jewels and deer made of jewels, as well as eighty-four thousand fans;
and she presented eighty-four thousand elixirs to the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ratnagarbha.
And he spoke thus: "O Blessed One, I have many duties and much to do;
may the Blessed One forgive me, and may you take your pleasure in our grove."
“May the Blessed One always delight in this grove;
I shall come again to the Blessed One for the purpose of seeing, venerating, and attending upon him.
And the thousand sons of King Araṇemin, having prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One, each addressed the Blessed One as follows:
—"May the Blessed One consent; each one of us will attend upon the Blessed One for three months, together with the community of monks, providing all necessary requisites.
The Blessed One consented to those thousand princes by remaining silent.

Knowing that they had accepted [the invitation], King Araṇemi then bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, circumambulated the community of monks three times, and departed from the presence of the Blessed One.
Then, among those princes, the eldest, named Animiṣa, attended upon the Blessed One and the community of monks for three months with such service as this.
For example, King Araṇemin, as well as a thousand royal princes headed by Animiṣa, approached the Blessed One day after day to behold him, and to hear the Dharma from the Saṅgha of monks.
Furthermore, noble son, the father of the Blessed Tathāgata Ratnagarbha was a brahmin named Samudrareṇu;
having wandered throughout the entire Jambūdvīpa, he begged for alms-food from men, women, boys, and girls.

Having received that alms-food, he establishes the entire world of inhabitants of Jambūdvīpa in the taking of the three refuges; having so established them, he causes them to generate the mind set upon unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
As he wanders in this manner, there is no one in Jambūdvīpa who has become a human being [who does not receive his gift].
There is no one who has not been sustained by the alms-food of the brahmin Samudrareṇu,
nor anyone who has not been established in the going for refuge to the Three Jewels, nor anyone in whom the thought of unsurpassed perfect enlightenment has not been generated.
Or he who has not been encouraged to take up or established in supreme knowledge;

yet many hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of living beings have been established in the practices of the three refuges, and likewise encouraged, introduced to, and established in unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Prince Animiṣa also attended upon the Blessed One and the community of monks for three months with such service as King Araṇemin had done;

and at the end of those three months, he offered eighty-four thousand wheel-treasures, all made of gold, as well as divine cities, and the [seven] treasures of elephants, horses, jewels, women, householders, and counselors— setting aside eighty-four thousand elephants and horses.

In this manner, they each offered eighty-four thousand items to the Blessed One and likewise to the community of monks: sun-crystal gems, maidens, young princes, wish-fulfilling trees, heaps of flowers, parasols, garments, garlands, ornaments, jeweled thrones, crest-jewels, eye-ornaments, earrings, golden threads, pearl necklaces, sandals, couches, footstools, vessels, drums, conchs, kettledrums, banners, water-pitchers, lamps, bowls, and so forth; as well as various birds made of jewels, various animals made of jewels, and elixirs of immortality.
Then that prince asked forgiveness from the Blessed One and the community of monks;
with unblinking eyes, Prince Animiṣa attended upon the Blessed One together with the community of monks in such a manner, and just as King Araṇemin had done, he gave infinite offerings.
In this way, the Blessed One was attended by Indra’s host for three months, and his wealth was relinquished;
[the rest is] as before, and likewise for Anaṅgaṇa.
Fearless,
unclad,
unborn.
Drowsiness, blinking, and softness.
The Paṅgagaṇa, the Mādhvava, and the Mānava.
O you who possess the month,
O you who possess the spring,
O you who possess the flow.
One who follows commands, one who speaks with the mouth, and one who has much wealth.
Alindra, Nerava, and Reṇaja.
Candranemi, Sūryanemi, Indranemi,
Vajranemi, Kṣāntinemi, Sthānanemi.
Javanemi,
Raṇemi, and Rāhu.
Rāhubala, Rāhucitra, and Dāmacitra.
rājadhānaḥ,
rāgabhramaḥ,
rāndhavaḥ.
The protector,
the body,
and those who lie down.
yatravaḥ,
syajalaḥ,
yārmathaḥ.
yadhvajaḥ, yamānaḥ,
yasyanaḥ.
From Namajyotis to Arañjanadhva, as far as King Araṇemin, each of his thousand sons [offered] a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Ratnagarbha. (KpSū 64)

Together with an immeasurable community of monks, he attended upon the Blessed One with such service as robes, alms-food, bedding, seats, and medicinal requisites for the sick; for three months, just as the eldest prince had done,
each one likewise presented eighty-four thousand golden wheels, and so on in detail, up to eighty-four thousand elixirs of immortality, to the Blessed One and the community of monks.
Having made their vows with such great faith, some prayed for the state of a deity, some for the state of Śakra, some for the state of Māra,

some for the sovereignty of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*), some for great wealth, some for the vehicle of the disciples (*śrāvakayāna*), and some for the vehicle of the solitary buddhas (*pratyekabuddhayāna*); and while being empowered, they sought forgiveness from the Blessed One for two hundred and fifty-five years.

And at that time, the brahmin Samudrareṇu, the chief domestic priest, arrived and saw the Blessed One attended by those princes; having seen him, he invited [the Buddha] and the community of monks for seven years with all necessary provisions—
namely, robes, alms-food, bedding and seats, and medicinal requisites for the sick.

The Blessed One consented to his father’s chief priest by remaining silent. Then the brahmin Samudrareṇu attended upon the Blessed One with such service as was provided with every requisite, together with the community of monks, with robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
Then, noble sons, at another time, this reflection arose in the mind of the brahmin Samudrareṇu:
"I have indeed exhorted many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of living beings toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
yet I do not know the vow of this King Araṇemin."

"What does he seek? Does he desire the state of a god, or the state of Śakra, or the state of Māra, or great wealth, or the vehicle of the śrāvakas, or the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, or supreme perfect enlightenment?
Might it be that I have awakened to supreme perfect enlightenment?"
May I ferry across those beings who have not crossed over;
may I liberate those who are not liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair;
and may I lead to final nirvāṇa those beings who have not attained final nirvāṇa.

"May Your Majesty inform me in a dream— whether it be a god, a yakṣa, a nāga, a Buddha, a disciple, or a brahmin— what he desires: is it the glory of a deity, or the glory of a human, or the state of a disciple, or the level of a pratyekabuddha, or perhaps unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment?"
Then, noble son, the brahmin Samudrareṇu, the chief priest, saw such a radiance in a dream,
by which radiance he beheld the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, in Buddha-fields in the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā.
And those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, sent lotuses to that brahmin— lotuses with golden petals, silver stalks, beryl centers, and emerald filaments.
And upon all those lotuses, a solar disc was seen;
above each solar disc stood an umbrella made of the seven precious gems.
From each solar disc, sixty koṭis of rays issued forth, and all those rays entered the mouth of that brahmin.
He perceives his own body to be one thousand yojanas in measure, perfectly pure like a polished mirror-disk.
Within the belly of his own body, he sees six hundred thousand nayutas of koṭis of bodhisattvas seated cross-legged upon lotuses, absorbed in meditation.
He also sees those forms of the sun as garlands upon his own head.
He sees a parasol situated above in the sky, extending as far as the limit of the Brahma-world;
he sees various lotuses situated all around it.
And from those lotuses there issue forth divine musical instruments, surpassing those of humans, which he hears;
and there he sees King Āraṇemin running with a body smeared with blood, having the face of a boar, devouring various and numerous living beings.
Having devoured them, he sat at the foot of an *eraṇḍa* tree;
various living beings gathered and devoured that king until they had reduced him to nothing but a skeleton, and then cast him away.

In this manner, appearing again and again in the same way, with a body smeared with blood, he sat at the foot of the *eraṇḍa* tree after devouring many kinds of living beings, his face like that of a boar.

Having been devoured by various creatures until nothing remained but skeletons, they were cast aside. Furthermore, he saw princes with the faces of boars, others with the faces of elephants, others with the faces of buffaloes, others with the faces of lions, others with the faces of wolves, others with the faces of jackals, others with the faces of dogs, and others with the faces of monkeys.

He sees various kinds of living beings whose limbs and faces are drenched in blood; having devoured them, they sit at the foot of castor-oil trees, being devoured in turn by various creatures until only their skeletons remain, yet having been cast off, they stand once more in that very same body and devour living beings in the same manner.
He also sees other princes mounted on buffalo-carts, adorned with *sumanā* flowers.
As he was traveling along a wrong path toward the south,
Śakra, Brahmā, and the World-Protectors came and said to the brahmin:
“Brahmin, divide these lotuses into portions.”
Having divided them, first give one lotus as a share to the king; then give one lotus each to these princes;
and give the remaining ones to the provincial kings.
Having heard another [request] from the people, the brahmin said,
"As the gods command."
Then that brahmin, while he was still dividing the lotuses, woke up; reflecting upon this, he rose from his seat and thought again:
"This universal monarch has made a lowly vow; he delights in the pleasures of saṃsāra, and his inclination is base, being in common with the worldly."

Furthermore, O princes, there are some princes who aspire to the vehicle of the disciples (*śrāvakayāna*), whom I saw mounted on buffalo chariots, adorned with *sumanā* flowers, proceeding toward the south;
and [there is also] that great sacrifice which I have undertaken for the sake of all sentient beings.

And because, while wandering throughout Jambūdvīpa for a hundred years, I have established all sentient beings in unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; and because, in this manner, I have incited, introduced, and established many hundreds of thousands of nayutas of koṭis of living beings throughout the entire Jambūdvīpa in the three bases of meritorious action—
it is for this reason that I saw such a great radiance in my dream.

I have beheld the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, in the ten directions; and having wandered throughout the entire Jambudvīpa, I have solicited alms from men, women, boys, and girls, establishing, training, settling, and firmly grounding many hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of living beings in the practices of the three refuges.

And because I invited the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, together with the community of monks, to provide for all his needs for seven years, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, from other Buddha-fields in the ten directions sent lotuses to me.
And because I made a vow for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, [the Buddhas have honored me].
Therefore, those Buddhas dispatched parasols made of the seven precious gems;
furthermore, I saw forms of the sun upon those lotuses, and I saw rays of light entering my mouth.
That great physical form which was seen, the garland of sun-like bodies which was seen,
and those hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of Bodhisattvas within the womb, seated cross-legged upon lotuses and absorbed in meditation—
Such dreams as these were seen by me; and Śakra, Brahmā, and the World-Protectors appeared to me, commanding, "Divide these lotuses," and those lotuses were divided and given away by me.
"What if I were to relate these dreams to the Blessed Buddha?
What is their cause, what is their condition, that such dreams as these have been seen by me? What if I... (KpSū 70)
“I shall question the Tathāgata.
Then, at the end of that very night, the brahmin Samudrareṇu prepared food and went to where the Blessed One was early in the morning.
Having approached, he personally provided water for washing the hands to the Blessed One and to the community of monks.
Having provided water for washing the hands, he personally satisfied and served him with abundant hard and soft foods;

having thus satisfied and served him, and having in many ways satisfied and served the community of monks, and perceiving that the Blessed One and the community of monks had finished eating, washed their hands, and set aside their bowls, he took a low seat and sat before the Blessed One.
He sat down before him to listen to the Dharma.
Then King Araṇemin arrived at that very place, accompanied by his thousand sons and surrounded and escorted by many thousands of living beings;
he proceeded by carriage as far as the ground would allow for a vehicle, then alighted from the carriage and entered the grove on foot.

Having entered, he approached the place where the Blessed One was; having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and the community of monks, and sat down before the Blessed One to hear the Dharma.
Then the brahmin Samudrareṇu reported to the Blessed One the dreams exactly as they had appeared.
The Blessed One said: "Brahmin, as for that great radiance which you saw, by which radiance Buddha-fields equal in number to the sands of the river Gaṅgā were illuminated—"
The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, having seen you, have sent forth lotuses;

upon those lotuses, forms of the sun are seen emitting rays, and those rays enter into your mouth. O Brahmin, because you wandered through Jambudvīpa for a hundred years in the Adhatrika region, [the Buddhas have acted thus].

By that, you have established and settled beings beyond counting in the three bases of meritorious action; and you have inspired, settled, and established beings beyond counting in unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
And because you have undertaken this great sacrifice for the sake of all sentient beings, O Brahmin, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, will prophesy your attainment of unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

Those who reside, dwell, and maintain themselves in the world systems of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, and who teach the Dharma— by whom these lotuses were sent forth, with golden petals, silver stalks, lapis lazuli pericarps, and emerald filaments— and upon all those lotuses, forms of the sun are seen.

This is the precursor to that dream which you, O Brahmin, saw: that in the ten directions, in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who currently reside, remain, and maintain themselves, and who teach the Dharma— by those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, parasols made of the seven precious jewels were sent forth.
The parasols which remain suspended in the sky above,
reaching as far as the Brahmā world;

on the very night that you, O Brāhmaṇa, shall awaken to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, on that same night a sublime [light] shall appear in world-systems in the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā.
Fame, renown, and verses of praise arise and ascend, reaching as far as the Brahma-world; even by the gods, beginning with Brahmā, it is impossible to look upon the crown of his head.
This is the preliminary sign of that dream.
O Brāhmaṇa, as for that great physical form you have seen, extending as far as the Brahma-world, and as for that garland of sun-disks bound upon your head—

that is because those beings beyond counting whom you have inspired toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment will, once you have awakened to enlightenment, O Brāhmaṇa, attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment while remaining in worlds in the ten directions equal in number to the atoms within a Buddha-field.
All those whom you have inspired toward awakening will constantly proclaim your praise, saying:

"We were first inspired toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening by this Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; it is by him that we have now fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening."
And this is our spiritual friend.
Those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, will dispatch Bodhisattvas for the purpose of making offerings to you;
then those Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas—
Having performed worship of you with various miraculous displays of a bodhisattva,
and having heard the Dharma from you there, they will attain various kinds of meditative concentrations (*samādhi*), mnemonic formulas (*dhāraṇī*), and patient acceptances (*kṣānti*).
Those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, having gone to their respective buddha-fields, will proclaim your praises and cause your fame to be heard.
O Brahmin, this is the prior sign of that dream:
that you saw in your dream hundreds of thousands of myriads of kotis of bodhisattvas entering your womb and sitting cross-legged upon lotuses, absorbed in meditation.

And once you have attained perfect awakening, O Brahmin, you will inspire many hundreds of thousands of myriads of kotis of living beings toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment and establish them in non-retrogression regarding unexcelled,
perfect enlightenment.
When you have entered final nirvana through the unsurpassed parinirvana, O Brahmin, [those beings] in Buddha-fields as numerous as the atoms of dust in [all worlds]...

In the future, during the ten directions and in other buddha-fields, those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, while exercising their sovereignty through the Dharma, will speak your praise: "Thus, after incalculable eons have passed, there was a Tathāgata named such-and-such, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha."

“By that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, we were encouraged toward, disciplined in, introduced to, and established in unexcelled perfect enlightenment; and by him we were made irreversible, so that we have now fully awakened to unexcelled perfect enlightenment and have attained the kingdom of Dharma.”
"O Brahmin, this is the precursor to that dream.

As for what you saw in the dream, O Brahmin— those who, with faces like pigs up to those with faces like dogs, their bodies smeared with blood, having devoured various kinds of living beings, sat down low at the root of an *eraṇḍa* tree, along with others of diverse kinds— "

They are devoured by living beings until they are reduced to mere skeletons and cast aside; then, their bodies restored and smeared with blood, they devour various kinds of living beings with mouths like dogs until they are again seated at the foot of a low eranda tree,
where they are eaten by diverse creatures.

Those deluded men have been incited and established by you in the three bases of meritorious action—namely, in generosity, restraint, and self-control—and they now long for the suffering of falling from the celestial realms;

for among humans, they long for the sufferings of old age, sickness, death, association with the unpleasant, and separation from the pleasant; and among the hungry ghosts, they long for the suffering of hunger and thirst.
They long for the suffering of devouring one another among animals, and the suffering of burning, cutting, killing, binding, and various forms of torture in the hells.

Established in the three bases of meritorious action, they desire sovereignty as kings of the gods among the devas, and they crave lordship over a single continent among humans. Therein, all sentient beings become their objects of enjoyment.
And they too shall become the sustenance for the enjoyment of all sentient beings.
Thus, all those deluded men, having been established by you in the three bases of meritorious action, will become your lay disciples (*upāsakas*).

"Brāhmaṇa, this is the precursor to that dream. As for the other men you saw in your dream, mounted on buffalo-chariots with their heads adorned with garlands of *sumana* flowers, traveling by a wrong path toward the south—those sons of good family, Brāhmaṇa, have been established in the three bases of meritorious action; they have set out upon the vehicle of the Śrāvakas solely for the sake of self-subduing and self-pacification."
“O Brāhmaṇa, this is the preliminary sign of those individuals who have set out upon the Śrāvaka vehicle.”
Then, noble son, the brahmin Samudrareṇu said this to King Āraṇemin: "Great King, human birth is difficult to obtain;

the perfection of the opportune moment is difficult to obtain; and the appearance in the world of Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones—who are like the flower of the udumbara tree—is difficult to obtain."
Zeal for wholesome qualities is difficult to find; a right aspiration is difficult to find.
O Great King, the status of a king of gods is a source of suffering.

Great King, even the sovereignty and kingship over one or two continents among humans is a source of the arising of suffering; likewise, kingship over two, three, or four continents is a source of the arising of suffering.
Great King, for a long time you must experience the suffering of saṃsāra.
"Great King, the prosperities of gods and humans are unstable and as fickle as the force of the wind.
Like the moon reflected in water, fools—insatiable with the five strands of sensual pleasure and intoxicated by sense objects—long for the glory of gods and men.
Yet those fools experience again and again the suffering of torment in the hells, the suffering of delusion among animals, and [the suffering] among the hungry ghosts."
The suffering of hunger and thirst among humans, the suffering of separation from loved ones among gods, the suffering of death and decline, the suffering of dwelling again in a womb,
the suffering of being crushed under one another's heads, and the suffering of devouring one another—
thus do the foolish, wandering about, experience suffering.
For what reason?

Because those who are deprived of spiritual friends do not make the right aspiration, nor do they exert themselves for the attainment of what has not been attained, for the realization of what has not been realized, or for the direct realization of what has not been directly realized. Thus these foolish, childish people weary themselves over the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), wherein all suffering comes to an end.
And they do not grow weary of nor are they terrified by cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), wherein suffering arises again and again.
Examine this, O Great King, how cyclic existence is the vessel for all sufferings.
Therefore, O Great King, you who have performed your duties in the teaching of the Blessed One, planted roots of merit, and gained faith in the Three Jewels—

"O Great King, having given gifts to the Blessed One, you will attain great wealth; having guarded your moral discipline, you will obtain rebirth in heaven; and having heard the Dharma from the presence of the Blessed One, you will obtain the great Dharma of wisdom. These things shall be fulfilled for you. Furthermore, O Great King, you have performed sacrifices and have generated the mind set upon unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment."
He said, "Enough, Brahmin!
Being one who delights in cyclic existence, I do not desire unexcelled perfect enlightenment for the sake of becoming a brahmin.
Great Brahmin, as for the gift I have given, the ethical discipline I have guarded, and the Dharma I have heard—"
“Indeed, O Brāhmaṇa, unsurpassed perfect enlightenment is difficult to attain. A second time, the Brāhmaṇa Samudrareṇu said to the king: “Great King, the path to enlightenment is pure;
one must make a vow with a sincere intention.”
Being fully confident, that path is purified by its resolute intention;
that path is straight and free from deceit;
that path is pure because it carries away the flow of afflictions.
That path is vast because it is free from blemish;
that path leads to convergence for the sake of reflection;
that path is fearless because of the non-performance of all evil.
That path is very soft through the perfection of generosity;
that path is cool through the perfection of ethical discipline;
that path is without dependence through the perfection of patience.
That path has its basis in the foundation through the perfection of vigor;
that path is untroubled through the perfection of meditation;
that path is well understood.

That path is perfectly serene through the perfection of wisdom; that path is followed by the knowledge of intrinsic nature through great loving-kindness; and that path is accompanied by great compassion.
That path is always gladdened by great sympathetic joy;
that path is undefiled by equanimity;
that path is free from thorns consisting of thoughts of sensual desire, ill will, and cruelty.
That path leads to security because of the absence of obstructed thought;
that path is free from rogues because of the thorough knowledge of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles;
that path has struck down Māra and his adversaries because of the careful investigation of the elements and sense-bases.
That path is easy to awaken to, because it is free from the obscuration of the darkness of ignorance.
That path leads the minds of beings with firm vigor, because it is devoid of the mental preoccupations of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
That path is enduring, because it is sustained by the empowerment of all the Tathāgatas.
That path produces great jewels because it is conducive to the jewel of omniscience;
that path is constantly illuminated by the Blessed One’s unimpeded gnosis; and that path is practiced by those who teach the roots of virtue because it is sustained by all the Tathāgatas.
That path is free from that which accords with the defilements of evil, because it has abandoned attachment and aversion;
that path is one where dust is destroyed, because it is devoid of malice, stubbornness, and anger;
that path leads to a happy rebirth, because it is separated from all unwholesome states.
“O Great King, the path to awakening leads to security and culminates in nirvāṇa.
O Great King, generate the mind of awakening!
The king said, “Brahmin, this Tathāgata appeared in the world when the lifespan of beings was eighty thousand years.”
It is not possible for the Tathāgata to pacify all states of woe.
Those beings who have planted roots of merit abide in the fruit;
some have attained perfection in meditative concentration, mnemonic formulas, and patient acceptance.
Those beings who possess superior roots of virtue have become irreversible from enlightenment;
some, having planted roots of virtue, experience the splendor of gods and humans.
Beings wander about according to their own respective wholesome and unwholesome karmas.
Which beings have been disciplined by the Blessed One such that not even the suffering of a single being has been pacified?
He is merely a field-like support for the Blessed One; he does not effect the liberation from suffering for those beings who have not previously planted roots of merit.
I generate the mind of awakening;

by practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva through this accumulation of great wisdom and this inconceivable, sublime entrance into the gateways of the Dharma, may I discipline sentient beings and perform the work of a Buddha.
It is not only in this defiled buddha-field that I shall set my mind upon awakening.
I shall dedicate [this merit].
If I should obtain such a buddha-field and generate the thought of awakening, then I shall practice the conduct of a bodhisattva until I touch unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
"And may I pacify all the suffering of sentient beings in that buddha-field.
Then, noble son, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ratnagarbha performed such a miraculous feat and entered the samādhi called *ādarśavyūha* (Array of the Mirror).
When the Blessed One was thus absorbed in the *ādarśavyūha* samādhi, a manifestation of such a nature appeared.

By that radiance, in each of the ten directions, world-systems as numerous as the atoms in a thousand Buddha-fields— arrayed with all excellent qualities— are seen; in some, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, have passed into parinirvāṇa, and in others, they remain poised for parinirvāṇa.
Wherever bodhisattva mahāsattvas, seated at the foot of the Bodhi tree, defeat Māra;
wherever, having recently attained full awakening, they turn the wheel of Dharma;
and wherever, having recently turned the wheel of Dharma, they teach the Dharma.
Where the buddha-fields of the buddhas and bodhisattvas are manifest,
where there is no arising of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas,
and where śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do arise.
And where a Buddha-field is empty of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas;
or in some cases, a Buddha-field is afflicted, characterized by the five corruptions.
In some places it was completely pure, free from the five corruptions;
in some places the sentient beings were superior, and in others they were inferior.
In some places beings have long lifespans, and in others they have short lifespans;
some buddha-fields are destroyed by fire.
Some [are destroyed] by water, some by wind; in some cases they revolve.
In some places they remain turned away;
all of them are seen clearly illuminated by a sublime radiance. Having seen those arrays of qualities in that buddha-field, the entire assembly—
The brahmin Samudrareṇu spoke again to the king: “Behold, Great King, these magnificent arrays of qualities of the buddha-fields!
Generate, Great King, the mind set upon unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening!
Take hold, Great King, of a buddha-field such as you desire.”

Then King Araṇemi, having bowed with palms joined toward where the Blessed One was, addressed the Blessed One as follows: "By what karma, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva obtain a completely pure buddha-field, and by what karma an impure one?
By what karma are sentient beings superior?"
“...as long as the lifespan of sentient beings is extensive.

The Blessed One said: “By the power of his vow, O Great King, a bodhisattva mahāsattva takes hold of a completely pure buddha-field, free from the five corruptions; by his vow, he may take hold of one that is not completely pure.”
The king said, “Venerable Blessed One, having entered the city and sat down with one-pointed concentration, I shall contemplate a vow;
such a buddha-field as I desire— one free from the five corruptions— is pleasing to me, and therein I shall dedicate these practices of excellent conduct.”
The Blessed One said, "Now is the time for you, Great King, as you deem fit.
Then, noble son, King Araṇemi bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and, having circumambulated the community of monks three times, departed from the presence of the Blessed One.
Having entered the city, he sat down in his own home, secluded and with one-pointed mind.
He contemplates the array of the vow for a buddha-field.
Then, the brahmin Samudrareṇu addressed the eldest prince, Animiṣa:
"O Animiṣa, you must generate the mind set upon unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening."
"And whatever merit has been earned by you while practicing the three bases of meritorious action, dedicate all of that toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
He replied, "Preceptor, having gone to my own home, I too shall sit alone in seclusion and contemplate the magnificent array of qualities of a Buddha-field;
if the thought of enlightenment should arise, [I shall dedicate it]."
"Having returned to the presence of the Blessed One, I shall dedicate my thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*).

Thereupon, that prince also bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and circumambulated the community of monks three times; then, departing from the Blessed One’s presence, he went to his own residence, sat down alone in seclusion, and contemplated the array of qualities of a buddha-field.
Then, noble son, the brahmin Samudrareṇu, the chief priest, having invited the second prince, said to him: "O prince, generate the mind of awakening," and so on in detail, as before, up until—
He inspires all one thousand princes toward awakening, as well as eighty-four thousand local kings and ninety million other beings toward awakening.
They all said, "We too, having gone to our respective homes, shall sit alone and contemplate the array of qualities of a Buddha-field.
Having spoken thus, they all went to their own homes and sat alone for seven years, contemplating their vows regarding the array of qualities of a Buddha-field.
Then, noble son, at another time, this reflection arose in the mind of the brahmin Samudrareṇu:
"Indeed, I have exhorted many hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of living beings toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
And I have invited this Buddha, the Blessed One, together with an immeasurable saṅgha of monks, to provide all necessary provisions for seven years."

"And if my aspiration for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment is fulfilled, and if this vow of mine is accomplished— that I shall inspire the gods, asuras, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and kumbhāṇḍas to this great sacrifice."
Then, noble son, the brahmin Samudrareṇu, the royal chaplain, longed for a vision of Vaiśravaṇa.
Thereupon, the great king Vaiśravaṇa, surrounded and escorted by many hundreds of thousands of yakṣas, approached the place where the brahmin Samudrareṇu was.
Having arrived, he stood before the brahmin Samudrareṇu and said this: "Brahmin, what do you desire from me?"
The brahmin asked, "Who are you?
Vaiśravaṇa replied, "O brahmin, have you not heard that there is a lord of the yakṣas named Vaiśravaṇa?
I am he. Brahmin, what do you command? What shall I do?"
The brahmin said,
"Listen, Lord of Yakṣas, I shall perform worship of the Blessed One; you should apply yourself with zeal to this."

He replied, “Let it be as you desire, O Brahmin. “In that case, Great King, at our word, you should cause the yakṣas to be inspired toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; and furthermore, inspire them in this way:”
"If you yakṣas desire unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, go; bring from beyond the ocean gośīrṣa and uragasāra sandalwood.
Others, for the sake of the Blessed One, [bring] incense, and others various flowers."
“By means of this, I shall perform worship of the Blessed One day after day.

“So be it, brahmin,” replied Vaiśravaṇa, the Great King; having given his word to that brahmin, he vanished right there, struck the drum, assembled the yakṣas and rākṣasas, and said this to them: (KpSū 85)
—“Friends, you should know this: in Jambudvīpa there is a brahmin named Samudrareṇu, the chief domestic priest of King Araṇemin;
he shall attend upon the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ratnagarbha, together with the community of monks, for seven years with all necessary provisions.”
"Therefore, you should rejoice in that merit,

and by means of that root of goodness, you should resolve your minds upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. At that time, many hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of yakṣas and rākṣasas joined their palms and said:

“Whatever outflow of merit, whatever outflow of virtue belongs to the brahmin Samudrareṇu, who for seven years attended upon the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ratnagarbha with all necessary provisions, together with an immeasurable saṅgha of bhikṣus—
we rejoice in that entire mass of merit; and by that root of virtue, may we fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.”
The great king Vaiśravaṇa said: "Listen, sirs!

Whoever among you desires the roots of virtue or seeks merit, let him bring gośīrṣa and uragasāra sandalwood from beyond the ocean for seven years, so that the brahmin Samudrareṇu may prepare food for the Blessed One and the community of monks."
Then ninety-two thousand yakṣas proclaimed with one voice:
"Friends, for these seven years we shall bring gośīrṣa and uragasāra sandalwood,
by which the brahmin Samudrareṇu will prepare food for the Blessed One and for the community of monks."
Forty-six thousand yakṣas said,
"We shall bring the fragrance.
Fifty-two thousand yakṣas said:
“We shall bring various flowers,” said twenty thousand yakṣas. “We shall take the vital essence of various elixirs for the sake of the Blessed One and the community of monks.”
“Whatever food and drink shall be prepared there, we will infuse it with vital energy (*ojas*).
Seventy thousand *yakṣas* said,
“Friends, we shall prepare food for the sake of the Blessed One and the community of monks.”
Then, noble son, the brahmin Samudrareṇu desired to see the great king Virūḍhaka.

Thereupon, the great king Virūḍhaka went to where the brahmin Samudrareṇu was; having approached him, [he spoke], and as many as hundreds of thousands of nayutas of koṭis of kumbhāṇḍas generated the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

In this way, Virūpākṣa and Dhṛtarāṣṭra caused many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nāgas and gandharvas to resolve their minds upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. Then, by the power of the Buddha, the world-protectors from the second four-continent system came into the presence of the brahmin Samudrareṇu,
and the brahmin likewise exhorted them as well.
They too, having gone to their respective assemblies, incite them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
even unto a hundred koṭīs of Vaiśravaṇas together with their assemblies from throughout the triple-thousand great thousandfold world system, they incite them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
They exhorted one hundred koṭis of Vīrūḍhakas, one hundred koṭis of Virūpākṣas, and one hundred koṭis of Dhṛtarāṣṭras, together with their retinues, toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Then, noble son, this thought occurred to the brahmin Samudrareṇu:
"If I were to awaken to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, my hope would be fulfilled; and if my vow were to be fulfilled..."
On that day, I would cause the Virūḍhakas to perform their labor;
at this great sacrifice, I would distribute it among sentient beings and encourage them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
“If by this merit I should awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, may Śakra, the lord of the gods, approach me today to see me;
may the divine son Suyama, the divine son Saṃtuṣita, the divine son Sunirmita, and the divine son Paranirmitavaśavartin also approach to see me.
O noble son, as soon as that thought arose in the brahmin Samudrareṇu, Śakra, the lord of the gods, approached him to see him.
The devaputra Suyāma, the devaputra Saṃtuṣita, the devaputra Sunirmita, and the devaputra Paranirmitavaśavartin approached that brahmin to see him.
The brahmin Samudrareṇu questioned them.
“Who are the venerable ones? The five kings of the gods each proclaimed their own names and lineages, and spoke thus:
“O Brahmin, what do you command us?
What implements must we provide for this great sacrifice?
The Brahmin replied:

“Whatever most excellent jeweled gabled halls you have in the world of the gods, or jeweled trees, wish-fulfilling trees, fragrance trees, flower trees, or fruit trees; divine robes, divine seats, divine furnishings,
divine jeweled vessels, divine ornaments, parasols, banners, flags, and jewelry, and divine musical instruments— ”
“With those objects, adorn the entire Jambūdvīpa for the sake of the Blessed One and the community of monks.

“So be it, friends,” replied those five divine kings to the brahmin. Having given their word to the brahmin, they departed from his presence and went to the world of the gods; having arrived there, [they summoned] the divine son Veṭaka, the divine son Āveṭuka, the divine son Rohiṇa, and the divine son Korabhananda.
Addressing the sons of the gods, they spoke thus:
"Go, friends, descend into Jambudvīpa and adorn the Jambūvana grove with such distinguished ornaments and such arranged seats, so that it shall be adorned just as this world of the gods is."
“Build a jeweled gabled pavilion for the sake of the Blessed One exactly like this very jeweled gabled pavilion with its jeweled portico; friends, build a gabled pavilion such as this!

Having received the command from the king of the gods, those five sons of the gods descended to Jambudvīpa and, in a single night, adorned the entire Jambuvana grove with such ornaments—ranging from jeweled trees to banners—and constructed for the sake of the Blessed One a gabled pavilion of such a form as that jeweled portico of Śakra, the lord of the gods.
Having adorned the gabled pavilion and the entire Jambūvana grove with every form of perfection and with divine ornaments, they approached the kings of the gods and announced:
"O noble ones, you should know that just as this world of the gods is well-adorned, so too is the Jambūvana garden well-adorned with excellent divine ornaments and perfected in every aspect."
And such was this gabled hall made of all kinds of jewels for the sake of the Blessed One, just like the jeweled gabled hall of Śakra, the lord of the gods.
Indeed, friends, there is not the slightest difference between the world of the gods and Jambudvīpa, or between [the world of the gods] and the Jambūvana grove garden.
Then those five divine kings—Śakra, Suyāma, Saṃtuṣita, Sunirmita, and Paranirmitavaśavartin—descended to Jambudvīpa, approached the brahmin Samudrareṇu, and spoke to him as follows:
“O Brahmin, the Jambūvana grove has been adorned for the sake of the Blessed One and the community of monks.
What more is there for us to do?”

When this had been said, the brahmin Samudrareṇu spoke thus to the five sons of the gods: "O you five kings of the gods, you shall indeed exercise sovereignty over your respective divine assemblies; let your authority prevail there, O kings, and each of you shall convene your own assembly of gods in Jambūdvīpa."
"Go to see the Blessed One, to pay him homage, and to attend upon him, as well as the community of monks;
and listen to the Dharma from the presence of the Blessed One.
Then those five kings of the gods, having gone to their respective abodes, [informed] Śakra, the lord of the gods, and the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
Having assembled, they spoke thus: "Friends, you should know that in Jambudvīpa there is a brahmin named Samudrareṇu, the chief domestic priest of King Araṇemin;
he has invited the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha together with an immeasurable saṅgha of bhikṣus for seven years and honors him with all necessary provisions."

"We have also decorated this entire monastery for the sake of the Blessed One and the community of monks; therefore, out of appreciation for this root of merit, you should resolve your minds upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment through the exhortation of the brahmin Samudrareṇu.
At that time, many hundreds of thousands of nayutas of koṭis of deities from the Heaven of the Thirty-three, having raised their joined palms, uttered these words:

“Friends, we rejoice in such a mass of merit. By means of this rejoicing, whatever merit may accrue to us, we dedicate it all toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. Suyāma, the son of the gods, having assembled the Yāma gods—[the passage continues] in detail—the Tuṣita gods, and the Nirmāṇarati gods.

A son of the gods from the Paranirmita realm, having assembled the gods of the Paranirmitavaśavartin heaven, spoke these words with his palms joined together, along with many hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of sons of gods:
"Friends, we rejoice in whatever root of merit there is, and from that root of merit, we dedicate all that merit toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"Therefore, friends, let us go; let us descend to Jambudvīpa to see the Blessed One, to pay him homage, to attend upon him, and to hear the Dharma, as well as the community of monks.

Then those five divine kings, each one at night together with many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of gods—men, women, boys, and girls—descended to Jambudvīpa. Having bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and [the feet of] the community of monks, they [honored] the Blessed One.
They listen to the Dharma from his presence.

The gods, stationed in the expanse of the sky, scatter a rain of divine flowers— blue lotuses, red lotuses, white lotuses, water lilies, *sumanā*, *vārṣika*, *atimuktaka*, *campaka*, *māndārava*, and *mahāmāndārava*— upon the Blessed One,
and they play divine musical instruments.
Furthermore, noble son, this reflection arose in the mind of the brahmin Samudrareṇu:
"If my aspiration for unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening is to be fulfilled, [then let this sign appear]."

"Therefore, this vow of mine shall be fulfilled: that I may cause these asuras to be established in awakening. Noble son, as soon as that thought arose, the five lords of the asuras approached the place where the brahmin was; having approached, by the word of the brahmin, many hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of asuras—including women, men, boys, and girls—generated the resolve for unexcelled, perfect awakening.
Having approached the presence of the Blessed One, they listen to the Dharma—
the detailed account is as before—
and in this way, that brahmin awaits Māra.
Furthermore, at that time, a Māra named Pūrṇa arrived, along with many hundreds of thousands of nayutas of koṭis of Māra-host deities—

men, women, boys, and girls— and they all resolved their minds upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, until finally they approached to hear the Dharma. Then, noble son, the brahmin Samudrareṇu desired to approach the great Brahmā named Ketapuri.
Having received the promise from the presence of the Brahmin, [they descended] from the Brahma-world; then,

hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of living beings generated the resolve for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, and thereafter they descended to see, pay homage to, and attend upon the Blessed One and the community of monks.
And [he went] into the presence of the Blessed One to listen to the Dharma.

Then, O son of good family, the brahmin Samudrareṇu, in the second four-continent world-system, desired Śakra; he also desired to see the sons of the gods Suyāma, Saṃtuṣita, Sunirmita, and Paranirmitavaśavartin.
Those five kings of the gods also, through the power of the Blessed One, approached the presence of the brahmin, and the brahmin instructed them.
They too, having returned to their own abodes, exhorted their respective assemblies by means of the brahmin’s hand.
In this way, many hundreds of thousands of millions of deities of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven generated the resolve for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.

Together with their wives, men, boys, and girls, they have come to this world-system of four continents along with Śakra, in order to see, pay homage to, and attend upon the Blessed One and the community of monks,
and to hear the Dharma from the presence of the Blessed One.
In this way, the divine sons Suyāma, Saṃtuṣita, Sunirmita, and Paranirmitavaśavartin—

having exhorted the gods up to those of the Paranirmitavaśavartin realm toward awakening— arrived at the four-continent world-system accompanied by many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Paranirmitavaśavartin gods, including men, women, boys, and girls, who had all resolved their minds upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
To see, pay homage to, and attend upon the Blessed One and the community of monks, and to hear the Dharma from the presence of the Blessed One;
likewise, in the second four-continent world-system, there were the lords of the asuras, the Māras, and the Brahmās. (KpSū 94)

In this way, in the third four-continent world-system, and in the fourth and fifth, Śakra, Suyāma, Saṃtuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, Paranirmita-vaśavartin, the lords of the asuras, Māra, and the Brahmās— by the power of the Buddha— came to this four-continent world-system with their retinues in order to hear the Dharma.

Likewise, from as far as the trichiliocosm great thousandfold world-system, there came a hundred koṭis of Śakras, a hundred koṭis of Suyāmas, a hundred koṭis of Saṃtuṣitas, a hundred koṭis of Nirmāṇaratis, and a hundred koṭis...

There were a hundred koṭis of sons of the gods from the Paranirmitavaśavartin realm, a hundred koṭis of lords of the asuras, a hundred koṭis of Māras, and a hundred koṭis of Great Brahmas; each individual Great Brahma was accompanied by many hundreds of thousands of koṭi-niyutas of deities of the Brahmakāyika realm who had all generated the resolve for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Surrounded and escorted by them, through the power of the Blessed One, he came to this world-system of four continents to see the Blessed One,
to approach him, to pay homage, to attend upon him, and to hear the Dharma from the Blessed One and the community of monks.
At that time, there was no spot of ground in the great trichiliocosm that was not filled [by them].
Then, noble son, this thought occurred to the brahmin Samudrareṇu:
"If my aspiration for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment is to be fulfilled, then just as these hundreds of koṭis of Vaiśravaṇas, up to hundreds of koṭis of Mahābrahmās, follow after me, even so..."
The Blessed One accords with me;

for if he were to perform such a great miracle that the painful sensations of all humans, animals, those in the world of Yama, and those in the hells within this triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system would be stilled and pleasant sensations would arise.
"And before each one of them, a manifestation of a Buddha should stand, which would inspire those beings toward unexcelled,

perfect enlightenment. Then, noble son, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ratnagarbha, having known with his own mind the thought in the mind of the brahmin Samudrareṇu, at that moment entered the samādhi called Pratāpa.
Just as, with his mind in meditative concentration, from each and every pore of the Blessed One’s body while the Blessed One was in the *pratāpa* samādhi,
incalculable rays of light issued forth, and by those rays this great trichiliocosm world-system was suffused;
some of those rays went to the hells and blew warm winds upon the beings born in the cold hells.

For those beings who have been reborn in the hot hells, cool winds blow, by which all the suffering of hunger, thirst, and exhaustion of those hell-beings is pacified, and a pleasant sensation arises.

Furthermore, before each individual hell-being stands a manifested form of a Buddha, his body adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and his person further embellished by the eighty secondary characteristics.
Then, as those hell-beings are filled with happiness, this thought occurred to them:
“What is the cause for this cessation of our suffering and the appearance of this happiness?
Upon seeing the Blessed One, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and his body radiant with the eighty minor characteristics,
they spoke thus:
“By the power of this Greatly Compassionate One, this Great-Souled One, we have become so happy.
Born of joy and gladness, their minds serene, they gazed upon the Blessed One. To them the Blessed One said: “Excellent, you beings! Speak the words, ‘Homage to the Buddha!’”
"And generate the mind set upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
in this way, painful sensations will no longer arise for you,
and you will always be recipients of pleasant sensations."
They spoke thus:
"Homage to the Buddha! We generate the mind set upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
may this root of merit of ours lead to the exhaustion of our karmic obstructions."
Then, some who have passed away are reborn among the community of human beings.
For those hell-beings who are being burned by fire, those rays emit cool breezes;
touched by them, they become free from suffering, with their hunger and thirst completely stilled.
As many as there were who, having passed away from there, were reborn in the common lot of human beings—
in the same way this should be stated for those in the animal realm, and likewise for humans up to that point—
and that radiance, having returned, circled the Blessed One three times.

Having circumambulated the Blessed One, they vanished into his uṣṇīṣa; and upon seeing this, countless gods, humans, yakṣas, rākṣasas, nāgas, and asuras were established in the state of non-retrogression from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, while countless beings attained meditative concentrations, patient acceptances, and dhāraṇīs.

When the humans of Jambudvīpa heard that in the capital city of Śrutamañjura, the Jambūvana grove had been adorned by the gods with celestial ornaments and decorations for the sake of the Blessed One and the community of monks, they thought:
"What if we were to go and see it?
There we shall behold the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha and the community of monks."
"Having gone there, let us hear the Dharma from the presence of the Blessed One.

Now at that time, day after day, many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of gods, humans, men, women, boys, and girls were coming to the city of Mañjuraka to behold, approach, and attend upon the Blessed One and the community of monks.
And they were desirous of seeing that park.
That park had twenty thousand gates made of the seven precious gems.
At each gate of the park, five hundred jeweled thrones were prepared.

And within them, five hundred young brahmins were seated; those beings who went there and entered that park, those young brahmins caused them to go for refuge to the Buddha, caused them to go for refuge to the Dharma, caused them to go for refuge to the Saṅgha, [and established them] in the unsurpassed [state]. (KpSū 98)
They incited them toward *samyaksaṃbodhi* and caused them to generate the aspiration for it;
those who were seated nearby and those who were staying at a distance subsequently entered that park to see, pay homage to, and attend upon the Blessed One and the community of monks.
In this way, during those seven years, the brahmin Samudrareṇu, the chief priest, incited, trained, established, and settled countless gods in *anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi*.

Innumerable nāgas, asuras, yakṣas, rākṣasas, kumbhāṇḍas, gandharvas, pretas, piśācas, and even those in the hells— innumerable beings down to those in the animal realm— were exhorted, disciplined, introduced, and established in unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
After those seven years had passed, the brahmin Samudrareṇu set aside eighty-four thousand wheels, setting aside the divine wheel-treasure;
he set aside eighty-four thousand elephants adorned with ornaments of the seven jewels, setting aside the elephant-treasure;
and so on, until he presented eighty-four thousand chariots.
After the passing of those seven years, in King Araṇemina, no desire for passion arose,

no desire for hatred, no desire for delusion; no desire for kingship, no desire for wealth, no desire for sons, no desire for queens, no desire for food, no desire for drink, no desire for clothing, no desire for perfumes, no desire for vehicles, no desire for sleep, and no desire for self.
He did not follow the will of others;
for seven years he did not lay down his side,
nor did the perception of night arise within him.

The perception of day did not arise in him; nor did he produce the perception of forms, the perception of sounds, the perception of tastes, the perception of smells, or the perception of tactile objects.
And during those seven years, no physical fatigue arose in him.
Constantly, continuously, and uninterruptedly, in each of the ten directions, he beholds the arrays of qualities of a thousand Buddha-fields within world-systems as numerous as atoms in those fields;
yet Mount Sumeru does not come into the range of his vision,
nor do other mountains, nor the Cakravāḍa and Mahācakravāḍa ranges, nor the intermediate spaces between worlds, nor the sun and moon, nor the celestial palaces come into the range of his vision.
Just as he beholds that purified Buddha-field,
so too, beholding the arrays of qualities of the purified Buddha-field, he contemplates his vow;
just as King Araṇemi dwelt for seven years in such an abiding in the qualities of happiness.
He beholds such arrays of qualities of Buddha-fields,
sitting while contemplating the vow for the array of qualities of a completely pure Buddha-field.
Thus were the princes Animiṣa the eldest,
Nimu, and Indragaṇa.
In this way, the king’s entire retinue— the thousand sons, the eighty-four thousand vassal kings, and another ninety-two million beings— all likewise spent seven years alone in seclusion,
perceiving in each of the ten directions world-systems as numerous as the atoms in a thousand buddha-fields.
Throughout those seven years, not a single desire for passion arose in them, nor a desire for hatred, nor a desire for delusion.
Until weariness arose in them,
they continuously and constantly beheld, in each of the ten directions, arrays of qualities of Buddha-fields as numerous as the atoms in a thousand Buddha-fields;
yet Mount Sumeru did not come within the range of their vision.
Neither other mountains nor even divine palaces came within the range of their vision;
rather, just as they had seen those arrays of qualities of the Buddha-fields, they contemplated the vow for the array of qualities of a perfectly pure Buddha-field.
All of them dwelt for seven years in such an abiding in these qualities.
Some contemplate the array of qualities of a completely pure buddha-field; some contemplate the array of qualities of an impure buddha-field.
Then, indeed, the brahmin Samudrareṇu, knowing that those seven years had passed and concluded, presented the seven jewels.

Bowing with palms joined toward where the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ratnagarbha was, he addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Venerable Blessed One, I have inspired King Araṇemin to aspire for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment."
Having gone home, he sat alone in a secluded place, withdrawn in meditation,
and no human being was permitted entry there.
In this manner, those one thousand princes were inspired toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
In this very way, each having gone to his own home, sat alone in solitary retreat, and no one was permitted entry there.
In this manner, eighty-four thousand minor kings, as well as ninety-two other millions of living beings, were encouraged, introduced to, and established in unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Having each gone to their own respective homes, they sat down alone in seclusion and entered into meditative withdrawal (*pratisaṃlīna*),
and no one was permitted entry there.
May the Blessed One attend to this until King Araṇemin rises from that meditative withdrawal and comes here.
“May all those whom I have exhorted toward awakening also come here; may they uphold the immovable mind set upon unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening;
and may they receive from the Blessed One their prophecy, as well as their lineage, name, and buddha-field.
Then, noble son, the Tathāgata, Arhat Ratnagarbha—
The Perfectly Enlightened One entered the samādhi called "The Lord of Accomplishment.
As he remained thus absorbed, rays of light—blue, yellow, red, white, madder-red, and crystal-colored—issued forth from his mouth.
Relying upon these rays, a Brahmā-manifestation stood before those who were dwelling in solitary retreat and spoke as follows:
“Arise, friends! Approach the Blessed One for the purpose of seeing him, paying homage, and attending upon him, as well as the community of monks.
Friends, the seven-year sacrifice of the brahmin Samudrareṇu has concluded;
the Blessed One will proceed on his travels elsewhere.”
Then, all of them, impelled by those rays,
arose and urged King Araṇemin;
thus urged by them, he rose up and set forth.

As the king set forth, deities in the expanse of the sky played musical instruments such as kettledrums, clay drums, and war-drums. Then King Araṇemin, mounted upon his chariot and surrounded by his thousand sons, eighty-four thousand minor kings, and ninety-two million living beings, departed from the city to go into the presence of the Blessed One— to behold, pay homage to, and attend upon the Blessed One.
He traveled by carriage as far as the ground was passable for a carriage,
then descended from the carriage; having descended, he entered the Jambūvana grove on foot,
and having entered, he approached the place where the Blessed One was.
Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and the community of monks, and sat down to one side together with many tens of millions of living beings.
Then the brahmin Samudrareṇu said to King Araṇemin: "May Your Majesty rejoice in this:
that you have performed service to the Blessed One for three months with all necessary provisions, as well as for the immeasurable community of monks."
Various and diverse jewels were presented, as well as eighty-four thousand cities;
he then dedicated all that mass of merit associated with rejoicing and that mass of merit associated with renunciation toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
In this manner, he exhorted the king’s thousand sons, and likewise the eighty-four thousand vassal kings and many other millions of living beings.
By means of that mass of merit associated with rejoicing, they were inspired and established in unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. And he said: "Rejoice here; bestow this gift.
And he spoke further:
“By this gift, I do not desire the fruit of Indra’s abode nor the Brahma-world;
I do not even long for the splendor of sovereignty, which is as fickle as the swift force of the wind.”
By the fruit of this gift, which arises from my great devotion,
may I indeed attain incomparable awakening that brings mastery over the mind, and may I ferry across all sentient beings.
Thus ends the third chapter, on the relinquishing of gifts, in the *Śrī-Karuṇāpuṇḍarīka*.
(KpSū 105) Chapter Four: The Prediction for Bodhisattvas.
Then, noble son, this thought occurred to the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ratnagarbha:

“By this brahmin Samudrareṇu, many millions of living beings have been inspired, established, and settled in unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, and placed on the stage of non-retrogression; they must be prophesied by me, and their Buddha-fields must be shown.
Then, the Blessed One entered the meditative absorption called *Bodhicittāsaṃpramoṣa* (Non-forgetfulness of the Mind of Enlightenment).
And he manifested a smile;

by that manifestation of a smile, having illuminated infinite and boundless buddha-fields with a pervasive radiance, he revealed the array of qualities of the buddha-field to King Araṇemin and to many tens of millions of other living beings.

Then, at that time, bodhisattva mahāsattvas in Buddha-fields beyond counting in the ten directions, having seen that radiance, came to this world-system through the power of the Buddha in order to see, pay homage to, and attend upon the Blessed One and the community of monks.

Having performed worship to the Blessed One with various miraculous displays of bodhisattvas, and having bowed their heads at his feet and attended upon him, they sat down before him, desiring to hear the bodhisattva vow.
Then, noble son, the brahmin Samudrareṇu, the chief priest, said to King Araṇemin: "Great King, you should first choose the array of qualities for your own buddha-field.
Then King Araṇemin, having bowed with palms joined toward where the Blessed One was, addressed the Blessed One: "Blessed One, I am a seeker of awakening.

Whatever roots of merit I have gained from serving the Blessed One for three months with various kinds of requisites, and from serving the immeasurable saṅgha of monks—may that be dedicated by me toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening."
It has been dedicated. And, Blessed One, for these seven years I have contemplated the arrays of qualities of a buddha-field;
in that buddha-field where I shall awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, O Blessed One, there shall be no hells, no animal births, and no worlds of Yama.
And may those beings who pass away not be reborn in an evil destiny;
may all those beings there be of golden complexion,
and may there be no diversity among all those gods and humans there.
All beings there shall remember their past lives;

and all beings shall be endowed with such a divine eye that they may see hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas dwelling, maintaining themselves, and teaching the Dharma in other world-systems.
And may all sentient beings be endowed with such a divine ear that they may hear the Dharma being taught by hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas;
and may all sentient beings be endowed with such knowledge of the minds of others.
They would know the mental activities of those beings residing in many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddha-fields.
All those beings would be endowed with such skill in supernatural power that, by a single production of thought, they could traverse hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddha-fields.
Furthermore, there would be no beings there who possessed anything as a possession, being even mentally unattached to their own bodies.
May all sentient beings become irreversible from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
may all sentient beings be of miraculous birth;
and may there be no designation of "female" therein.
There, there would be no limit to the lifespan of sentient beings, except by the power of their own vows;
nor would even the name of anything unwholesome exist there for those beings.
In that buddha-field there would be no foul odor;
that buddha-field would be suffused with the fragrance of the Blessed One, which surpasses that of the divine,
and all sentient beings would be adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man.
May all sentient beings be bound to only one more birth, except for those who have made a specific vow;
and may all sentient beings there, through the power of the Buddha, attend upon transcendent numbers of Buddhas within a single morning.
To whatever extent they might desire to perform worship of the Buddhas through various kinds of bodhisattva transformations, those very things shall be accomplished for them;
they shall return with that very same morning meal,
and all sentient beings shall proclaim the Buddha-piṭaka.
May all sentient beings be endowed with the strength of Nārāyaṇa;
may no sentient being be able to grasp the limit of the description of the qualities and ornaments of that buddha-field, even with a divine eye;
and may all sentient beings there have attained the analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid).
They shall possess incalculable eloquence;
and for each individual bodhisattva, there shall be a measure of one thousand yojanas,
and that buddha-field shall be radiant.
And all around, incalculable arrays of qualities of Buddha-fields would be visible there;
and whatever beings were born therein would remain practitioners of celibacy until the end of enlightenment,
and all those beings would be worthy of homage from the world including the gods.
Until the very limit of enlightenment, may they never be deficient in their faculties;
and may the beings born there together attain the noble joy and happiness that transcends the divine;
and may all beings there be possessed of the convergence of roots of virtue.
And all sentient beings there shall wear new saffron robes;

and as soon as they are born there, those beings shall attain the Samādhi called "Well-Divided," by the attainment of which Samādhi they shall go to Buddha-fields beyond counting and attend upon the Buddhas, beholding them until the end of enlightenment.

And whatever bodhisattvas should be born there, whatever kind of arrays of qualities of a buddha-field they might desire, such arrays of qualities of a buddha-field they would see within those jewel-trees.
And as soon as they are born, those beings shall attain a samādhi, by the attainment of which [samādhi] in the ten directions...

In other Buddha-fields beyond counting, may those beings who are born there constantly behold the Buddhas as they remain and maintain their lives; and may they all possess robes, celestial palaces, ornaments, jewelry, complexion, and form exactly like those of the gods who dwell in the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Creations (Paranirmitavaśavartin).
In that buddha-field, there would be no dust, stones, or black mountains;
no Cakravāḍa or Mahācakravāḍa mountain ranges, no Sumeru, and no great oceans; and there, in every way and from every direction, there would be no sounds of hindrances, obstructions, or afflictions.
In that [Buddha-field], there would be no word for the hells, the animal realm, or the world of Yama; there would be no word for the unfavorable conditions, nor any word for suffering.
Blessed One, I desire a Buddha-field of such a nature.
Venerable Blessed One, I shall practice the difficult austerities of a bodhisattva until I have purified a Buddha-field with such qualities as these.
"In this way, O Venerable Blessed One, I shall exert human effort;
thereafter, I shall realize unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
And my Bodhi tree shall be ten thousand yojanas in height."
Seated there, may I, in a single moment and with a single thought-moment, fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment;
and may my radiance be immeasurable, illuminating hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddha-fields.
May my lifespan be immeasurable, consisting of hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of incalculable eons, such that it cannot be calculated by anyone except through omniscient knowledge.
And may my assembly of bodhisattvas be immeasurable, excluding śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, such that it cannot be calculated except through omniscient knowledge.
And when I have attained awakening, may the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, in immeasurable and incalculable other Buddha-fields, speak my praises, proclaim my renown,

and utter my fame; and when I have attained awakening, may all those beings in immeasurable and incalculable other Buddha-fields who hear my name, having dedicated their roots of merit toward that Buddha-field,
be reborn in my own Buddha-field.
Excepting those beings who have committed the acts of immediate retribution or who reject the true Dharma,
may beings in other world-systems beyond counting, desiring rebirth in my Buddha-field, generate the mind of awakening once I have attained enlightenment.
And there they should perform the dedication of their roots of merit;
and at the time of their death, may I stand before them, surrounded by a host of bodhisattvas;
and upon seeing me, may they generate joy and serene faith toward me.
May they eliminate all obscurations,
and after passing away, may they be reborn in our buddha-field.
And those bodhisattvas there who might desire to hear from me a teaching of the Dharma never heard before, they shall hear it exactly as they desire.

And when I have attained awakening, bodhisattvas in incalculable Buddha-fields shall hear my name; they shall become irreversible from unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening, and they shall attain the first patience, and likewise the second.

Whatever kind of meditative concentration and mnemonic formula (*dhāraṇī*) they might desire, may they obtain such meditative concentration and mnemonic formula. Furthermore, after my final nirvāṇa, in incalculable eons and in incalculable Buddha-fields thereafter,
may the bodhisattvas, upon hearing my name, attain supreme joy, serene faith, and gladness, directed toward me alone.

Paying homage, struck with wonder, they would extol my fame and renown; and when, having been a bodhisattva, I have fully accomplished the work of a Buddha, thereafter I would manifestly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and once I have so awakened, the bodhisattvas who have attained supreme faith would become recipients of the first, second, and third patiences.
May they obtain whatever kind of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and mnemonic formula (*dhāraṇī*) they desire, and may they behold them continuously until the end of awakening.
And when I have attained awakening, may those women in incalculable Buddha-fields hear my name.
Upon hearing it, they would attain supreme joy and gladness,
they would resolve their minds upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment,
and until the very end of awakening, they would never again receive a female body.
And after I have attained final nirvāṇa, throughout incalculable eons, those women who hear my name shall attain supreme joy, gladness, and serene faith;
they shall generate the resolve for unexcelled,
perfect enlightenment, and until the very end of awakening, they shall never again receive a female body.
“Venerable Blessed One, I desire such a buddha-field; and I desire such beings with purified intentions.
May I, Blessed One, awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in such a buddha-field.”
Then, noble son, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ratnagarbha gave his approval to King Araṇemin, saying:
“Excellent, excellent, Great King! Your vow is profound, Great King; you have grasped a perfectly pure buddha-field.”
