and may the boys and girls dwelling in the womb in that buddha-field experience happiness for seven days and nights in this manner.
And those women, while pregnant, would experience such happiness as that of a monk who has attained the second dhyāna;
nor would those beings be defiled by the impurity of the womb's filth.
And on the seventh day, they would be reborn endowed with supreme fragrance and the highest comfort;
moreover, that woman would not experience any suffering,
and having both descended into the lotus pond and bathed, that woman would regain such mindfulness as this.
By which one may attain the concentration of the excellence of detachment,
and by that concentration one may be completely liberated from the deeds of Māra.
She shall be constantly and always in a state of meditative concentration (*samāhita*).

Furthermore, whatever karma of such a nature was performed and accumulated in previous births— by which she would otherwise have had to experience female existence for many millions of eons— that female existence shall, through the realization of this concentration, come to be completely and utterly exhausted.
Until my final nirvāṇa, may they no longer obtain a female form.

And as for those beings who have performed and accumulated such karma that they would otherwise be reborn dwelling constantly in the womb for incalculable eons and must experience suffering—may they hear my name once I have attained awakening and obtain serene faith; having passed away from there, [may they be reborn in my buddha-field].

May they be born in my buddha-field and be reborn there by entering a womb; may all their karma be completely exhausted therein until the end of enlightenment, so that those beings who have planted roots of merit shall never again be reborn by entering a womb, but instead be reborn upon lotuses.
Those beings who have not planted roots of merit would be reborn through dwelling in a womb;

however, through the exhaustion of karma, neither women nor the state of dwelling in a womb would be known in my buddha-field. Those beings in that buddha-field would be endowed with absolute happiness. From *sumana* and *tāla* trees stirred by the wind, such delightful sounds would issue forth as the words "suffering," "impermanence," "non-self," and "emptiness."
They would issue forth;
and by that sound,
the humans there would attain the samādhi called Ulkāvatī, and by that samādhi, those beings would understand the profound dharmas that manifest as emptiness.
Furthermore, in that buddha-field there would be no sound associated with sensual desires.
And, O Venerable Blessed One, seated at the foot of the Bodhi tree, may I attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening in a single moment.
Once I have attained awakening, in that buddha-field the light of the sun and moon shall no longer be perceived.
Except for the closing of flowers;
and may I emit such a radiance that by means of it, with my divine eye, I might see the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, dwelling in other immeasurable and incalculable Buddha-fields.
And having attained awakening, may I teach the Dharma with such a voice that by means of that voice I might fill the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world-system.

And whatever beings may be there, may they all attain the recollection of the Buddha; and wherever they may go, whether walking, sitting, or turning about, may they constantly and continuously see me. Whatever doubts regarding the Dharma they may have concerning various phenomena, may those doubts vanish for them by the mere sight of me and the mere looking upon me.

And when I have attained awakening, may those beings in the immeasurable and incalculable Buddha-fields in the ten directions— whether they belong to the vehicle of the śrāvakas, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, or the unsurpassed vehicle— who hear my name or my praise, pass away from there and [be reborn in my land].
May they be reborn in my buddha-field;
having heard my Dharma there, those who belong to the vehicle of the śrāvakas may become arhats who meditate upon the eight liberations,
and those who belong to the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas may attain individual enlightenment.

And those bodhisattvas there who belong to the Mahāyāna, having heard the Dharma from my presence, may they obtain profound meditative concentration, patient acceptance, and dhāraṇīs; may they become irreversible therein from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
And may my saṅgha of śrāvakas be immeasurable, such that it could not be counted by anyone except the Tathāgata himself.
And when I have attained awakening, wherever I may go and wherever my soles may touch the earth, there let thousand-petaled lotuses, radiant with the color of gold, appear;

and may those lotuses, having gone to empty buddha-fields, utter the sound and proclamation of my praise; and may those beings, upon hearing the description of my name, my praise, and my fame, give rise to joy, serene faith, and gladness.
Having conceived faith, they would desire rebirth in my buddha-field and dedicate those roots of merit there;
having passed away from that place, they would be reborn in my buddha-field.

And may my community of disciples be free from the impurities of ascetics; may it be free from the speech of ascetics, free from the crookedness of ascetics, and free from the deceit of ascetics; may it be a pure assembly that values the Dharma, not material requisites, and not gain, honor, or praise.
That assembly would delight in impermanence, suffering, non-self, and emptiness, and being diligent in vigor, they would be intent on hearing the Dharma and leaning toward the Saṅgha.

Furthermore, those irreversible Bodhisattvas therein who have entered the future [stages] would regain mindfulness; having passed through births, they would speak discourses connected with the perfection of wisdom, such that until the limit of enlightenment, those teachings would not fall into oblivion.
“May I remain until I have attained awakening for ten thousand great eons,
and after my final nirvana, may the True Dharma remain for a thousand eons.
The Blessed One said, “Excellent, excellent, O noble man!”
"You have taken hold of a perfectly pure Buddha-field.
In a future time, after one incalculable eon as vast as the sands of the river Ganges has passed and the second has begun, you will become [a Buddha] named Akṣobhya in the eastern direction;
there, a thousandfold Buddha-field called Abhirati will come into existence."
"Endowed with such an array of qualities as you have made this vow,
there you shall fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment;
thus indeed you shall become a Tathāgata named Akṣobhya, even unto a Buddha, a Blessed One."

Akṣobhya said: "Venerable Blessed One, if such a wish of mine should be fulfilled, then may all beings in all world-systems—those comprised within the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, and those included within the category of 'beings'—all become possessed of a mind of loving-kindness, a mind free from enmity, and a mind free from turbidity; and may they experience such physical happiness as that of one established on the tenth stage."

“May all sentient beings be endowed with such physical and mental happiness as that by which the purity of intention through the abandonment [of defilements] occurs for a Bodhisattva who has entered the Lotus Samādhi.
And when I prostrate at the feet of the Blessed One with the five-fold limb salutation, may the entire earth become radiant with gold.”

And that noble son, O son of good family, prostrated with his five limbs at the feet of the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha; and at that moment, all sentient beings were endowed with such happiness as was established by their vow,
and at that time the entire earth appeared radiant with gold.

The Tathāgata Ratnagarbha said: “Arise, O Pravaramati, you who are as immovable as a wheel set in the palm of your hand! Having established many who were full of craving within a heart of compassion, you, O Śubhamati, shall become a Teacher in the world.”
(KpSū 175) Then, noble son, the brahmin Samudrareṇu addressed the tenth prince, named Himaṇi.
[The text continues: Prince Himaṇi made a vow of such a kind as was made by Akṣobhya.
“Venerable Blessed One, if such a wish of mine is not fulfilled, then may all sentient beings attain mental attention directed toward the Buddha as their object;
may the fragrance of uragasāra sandalwood appear in the hands of them all,
and may they all dedicate that fragrance to the forms of the Buddhas.”

The Blessed One said: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family! Noble is the vow you have made, in that you have established all sentient beings with hands of uragasāra sandalwood and have generated, through your intention, the mental attention directed toward the Buddha."

"Therefore, noble son, let your name be Gandhahastin. You shall become [the successor] to the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Akṣobhya, after the passing of incalculable eons equal to the sands of the river Gaṅgā, and when there remains a second incalculable eon equal to the sands of the river Gaṅgā."
“Gandhahasta, when the True Dharma has vanished after the [Buddha] has entered final nirvāṇa, on the seventh day you shall manifest supreme, perfect enlightenment in that world-system;
you shall become the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Suvarṇapuṣpa, and so forth, up to: Buddha, Blessed One.”

Gandhahastin also said: "Venerable Blessed One, if such a wish of mine may be fulfilled, then when I bow at the feet of the Blessed One with the five-pointed prostration, let a rain of campaka flowers fall upon the entire monastery.

O son of good family, as soon as the bodhisattva Gandhahastin bowed at the feet of the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha with the five-pointed prostration, a rain of campaka flowers fell upon the entire monastery.
The Tathāgata Ratnagarbha said:
“Arise, O you of preeminent virtue, whose mind is showered with fragrant rain!
Display this excellent and most sublime path of purity; establish the many wandering beings on the further shore, free from fear.”
Then, noble son, the brahmin Samudrareṇu addressed the eleventh prince, named Siṃha.
[The passage continues] as previously described: just as the vow had been made by Gandhahastin, he offered a jeweled banner to the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha.
The Tathāgata Ratnagarbha said: "Excellent, excellent, O noble man! Be known by the name Ratnaketu;
you, Ratnaketu, shall become [a Buddha] in the future."

"When one incalculable aeon, equal to the sands of the river Gaṅgā, has passed and another second incalculable aeon, equal to the sands of the river Gaṅgā, remains; when the Tathāgata Svarṇapuṣpa has entered final nirvāṇa in that world-system Abhirati and his True Dharma has disappeared; and after the passing of three intermediate aeons, that buddha-field shall be named Jayasoma."
"There you shall attain unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment and become the Buddha, the Blessed One named Nāgavinarditeśvaraghoṣa;
such shall be your buddha-field in its array of qualities, just like that of the Tathāgata Akṣobhya.
Ratnaketu said, "Venerable Blessed One, if my aspiration for such a form may be fulfilled, then when I bow at the feet of the Blessed One, may all sentient beings likewise obtain such mindfulness."

"Just as those bodhisattvas who have set out for great enlightenment, out of compassion for the sake of all sentient beings, having set out for perfect awakening, do not turn back; even so, noble son, when the bodhisattva Ratnaketu had bowed at the feet of the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha,
the sentient beings likewise attained such mindfulness, namely, that all sentient beings were established in a mind of compassion."
Then, noble son, the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha said to the bodhisattva Ratnaketu:
“Arise, O steadfast one, O wise one of supreme form! For the sake of sentient beings, you have made a very firm vow.”
You establish many people in minds free from passion; you shall become a supreme man, an excellent Buddha.”
In the same manner— and so on— the five hundred princes, preceded by Mārdava, made such a vow;
having made it, they embraced such arrays of qualities of a buddha-field as were vowed for by the bodhisattva Gaganamudra.
They have also taken hold of the magnificent arrays of qualities of their Buddha-fields,

and all have been prophesied by the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment: "In this very way, at one and the same time, you shall touch unexcelled, perfect enlightenment in various world-systems."
Four hundred other princes, by whom such a buddha-field as that of Vajracchedaprajñāvabhāsa had been taken up,
were all likewise prophesied by the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment in various other world-systems. Furthermore, eighty-nine other princes made a vow of this kind:
And such a buddha-field was thus embraced,
just as by Samantabhadra;
all eighty-four thousand minor kings each made their own distinct and distinguished vow.
Each of them has individually taken hold of the magnificent arrays of qualities of their own Buddha-fields;
and all have been prophesied by the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment,
such that they shall attain awakening at the same time in various world-systems.
In this very way, three hundred million beings each made their individual vows and each separately took hold of the arrays of qualities of their respective buddha-fields;
and all were prophesied by the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
“In this very way, you too shall at one and the same time realize unexcelled, perfect enlightenment in various world-systems.”
Then, noble son, the Brahmin Samudrareṇu had eighty sons who were brothers of the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha; their eldest was a young brahmin named Samudreśvarabhuvi.
Then, noble son, the Brahmin Samudrareṇu addressed the young brahmin Samudreśvarabhuvi.
“Accept, young man, the pure array of qualities of a buddha-field.
The young man Samudreśvarabhuvi said,
“Father, you yourself should be the first to roar the lion’s roar.”
Samudrareṇu said, "Son, you first make your vow;
afterwards, I shall make my vow.
He replied, "Shall I then accept a completely pure buddha-field, or rather, an impure one?"
The chief priest said: "Those bodhisattvas who are endowed with great compassion take possession of defiled buddha-fields;
they take as their disciples those beings whose dispositions are afflicted and whose views are perverted—just as you yourself understand, young man."
Then, noble son, the young brahmin Samudreśvarabhuvi approached the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha;
having approached him and stood before the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha, he spoke thus: "In this way, venerable Blessed One, I long for unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
When the lifespan of beings is eighty thousand years, may I touch supreme enlightenment. O Blessed One,

just as beings at present have weak passion, weak hatred, and weak delusion, and possess a mind of renunciation, seeing the fear and faults of saṃsāra, so too may the beings be in that buddha-field where I shall attain perfect awakening.
And may they go forth into homelessness in my presence,
and may I teach the Dharma to sentient beings by means of the three vehicles.
Venerable Blessed One, if such a hope as this should be fulfilled, then may the Blessed One grant me the prophecy of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

The Tathāgata Ratnagarbha said: "Young man, in a future time, when one incalculable aeon equal to the sands of the river Gaṅgā has passed and you have entered into the second incalculable aeon equal to the sands of the river Gaṅgā, during the eon named Utpalasantīraṇa, you shall become [a Buddha]."

"The world-system of four continents shall be named Baliṣṭha; when the lifespan of beings is eighty thousand years, you will attain awakening in this buddha-field and become the Tathāgata named Ratnakūṭa, up to being a Buddha, a Blessed One."
He said, “Venerable Blessed One, if such a wish of mine may be fulfilled, then let a rain of red pearls fall everywhere in this grove,
and let the five-fold musical ensemble emerge from all the trees.
And when, noble son, the young brahmin Samudreśvarabhuvi prostrated with his five limbs at the feet of the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha, then a rain consisting of red pearls fell everywhere in the grove.
And from all the trees, the five-fold musical ensemble resounded.
The Tathāgata Ratnagarbha said:
"Arise, O best of the steadfast, treasury of inexhaustible wisdom, compassionate toward sentient beings, seeker of their welfare, whose mind is filled with loving-kindness!"
May your pure intention be fulfilled; you shall become a Buddha in the world who acts for the benefit of sentient beings.
And the second son of the brahmin was named Saṃbhava;
he spoke in this manner, just like Samudreśvarabhu.

The Tathāgata Ratnagarbha said: "You too, young man, in the aeon called Utpalasanti, in this world-system of four continents, in the most powerful Buddha-field Vardhamāna, when the lifespan of beings is eighty thousand years, you shall become a Tathāgata named Vairocanakusuma, even unto a Buddha, a Blessed One."
[The same] applies to the others; the third, however, said: "Two thousand years hence, you shall become a Buddha, the Blessed One named Jyotigandha.
[The rest of] the prophecy is as before.
In this manner, the Tathāgatas Sumanas, Śailarāja, Saṃvṛtalocana, Brahmottara, Jambūcchāya, and Pūrṇamuttara [each prophesied].

Ratnaśaila, Samudragarbha, Nārāyaṇa, Śikhī, Kanakamuni, Munīndra, Kauṇḍinya, Siṃhavikrama, Jñānadhvaja, Buddhaśrava, Aparājita, Vikasitojjaya, Hiteṣī, Prajñāvabhāsa, Mahendra, Śāntaprajñākara, Nanda, Nyagrodharāja, Kanakalocana, Sahita, Sūryanandi, Ratnaśikhī, Sumetra, and Brahma.
Sunda, Brahmarṣabha, Praṇāda, Dharmacandra,
Arthadarśin, Yaśonandin, Yaśottara, Abhirūpa, Sugandha, Catura, Pravaralocana,
Sunijasta, Sārthavrata, Sumanoratha, Varaprajña, Kanakadhvaja, Sunetra, Devaśuddha, and Śuddhodana.

Sudarśana, Virūḍhadhvaja, Virūpākṣa, Brahmasvara, Śrīsaṃbhava, Śrīmahāviraja, Maṇibhadra, Mārīci, Śākyamuni, Ghoṣeśvara, Satyasaṃbhava, Śreṣṭha, Saṃbhavapuṣpa, Sukusuma, Akṣobhya, Sūryagarbha, Ratīśvara, Nāgadanta, Vajraprabhāsa, Kīrtirāja, Vyāghraraśmi, and Sanetyajñānasaṃbhava.
Gandhasvara, Sālendra, Nārāyaṇagata, and Jyotigarbha—
O son of good family, the one who was the very last among them, the son of the domestic priest named Vigatabhaya-saṃtāpa,
stood before the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha and said:

“Venerable Blessed One, these seventy-nine young brahmins have all been prophesied that they will fully awaken to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment during the two Vardhamāna eons of the Utpalasaṃtīraṇa kalpa.
Blessed One, I too generate the mind set upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
for the Utpalasaṃtīraṇa kalpa is now waning, Venerable Blessed One.”
"In this eon, may I be the very last one to touch the supreme, foremost enlightenment.
May the lifespan of those seventy-nine Buddhas, down to its final limit, be the same as my own single lifespan once I have attained enlightenment;
and may the number of those to be trained by them be exactly the same as the number to be trained by me alone."
And just as they might teach the Dharma by means of the three vehicles,
and just as they might have a community of disciples, so great shall be my single community of disciples when I have attained awakening.
"And those beings who, during the arising of those seventy-nine Buddhas, were to obtain human birth in that *utpalasaṃtīraṇa* eon—
when the eon was coming to an end— may I, having awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, establish all those beings in certainty through the three vehicles.
Venerable Blessed One, if such a wish of mine may be fulfilled, then, Venerable Blessed One, grant me the prophecy of unsurpassed perfect enlightenment."
Then, noble son, the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha gave his approval to Vigatabhayasaṃtāpa:
"Excellent, excellent, O worthy man! You have arisen as a compassionate benefactor for beings beyond counting."

"Young man, in the future, when one incalculable eon equal to the sands of the river Gaṅgā has passed and a second incalculable eon equal to the sands of the river Gaṅgā has begun, at that time, when the aeon called Utpalasaṃtīraṇa is coming to an end, you shall be the very last to awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment."
"You shall become a Tathāgata named Viyagatarajasamudgatābhyudgatarāja, a Buddha, a Blessed One;
and just as the lifespan of those seventy-nine Buddhas will be half a kalpa,
so too shall your own lifespan be half a kalpa."
“Until all those aspirations of yours are fulfilled exactly as they were made.

He said, “If, O Venerable Blessed One, such a wish of mine may be fulfilled— that when I bow at the feet of the Blessed One with the five-fold prostration, then blue flowers of supreme fragrance shall rain down everywhere throughout this Buddha-field— ”
And whatever sentient beings should smell that fragrance, may the elements of all of them become serene and harmonious, and may all their diseases be pacified.

And when, O son of good family, the youth Vigatabhayasaṃtāpa prostrates with his five limbs at the feet of the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha, then a rain of blue flowers falls everywhere throughout that buddha-field.
And those beings who smelled that fragrance, all their elements became balanced, harmonious, and stable; and all those beings there became free from disease and possessed of little affliction.
The Tathāgata Ratnagarbha said:
“Arise, O you whose mind is tamed by the vow of compassion! You shall worship many Lords of the World;
you shall sever the firm bonds of the afflictions of the deceitful, and you shall become a treasury of auspicious and excellent wisdom.”

And, noble son, three koṭis of that brahmin’s disciples were seated at the gate of the grove; they established the beings who came there in the taking of the three refuges and exhorted them toward awakening.
Then, the brahmin Samudrareṇu addressed those disciples:
“O young brahmins, generate the mind set upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment!
Take up the qualities of a buddha-field as you desire;
make your vow before the Blessed One exactly as you wish.”
There was a young brahmin named Jyotīṣka, who asked: "By what kind of path, by what kind of equipment, by what kind of conduct, and by what kind of mindfulness is awakening attained?
The priest replied: "Young man, these four inexhaustible treasuries must be fully accumulated by a bodhisattva who has set out upon the path to awakening."
Which four?
"The inexhaustible accumulation of merit,
the inexhaustible accumulation of wisdom,"
The accumulation of wisdom is inexhaustible; the accumulation for the full realization of all dharmas is inexhaustible.
Such, noble son, is the path.
And thus, young man, the Tathāgata has spoken of the Dharma-door for crossing over saṃsāra called "The Compendium of the Purification of Requisites":
those bodhisattvas who relinquish the requisites of giving,
that leads to the maturation of beings who are to be trained.
The equipment of ethical discipline of bodhisattvas leads to the fulfillment of their vows;
the equipment of patience of bodhisattvas leads to the perfection of the primary and secondary marks; the equipment of vigor of bodhisattvas leads to the accomplishment of all desires.
The equipment of meditative concentration leads Bodhisattvas to the state of having a mind like that of a well-bred horse;
the equipment of wisdom leads Bodhisattvas to the thorough knowledge of all afflictions; the equipment of learning leads Bodhisattvas to unimpeded eloquence.
The equipment of merit for bodhisattvas conduces to being a source of sustenance for all sentient beings;
the equipment of knowledge for bodhisattvas conduces to the state of unerring knowledge;
the equipment of tranquility for bodhisattvas conduces to the workability of the mind.
The equipment of insight leads bodhisattvas to the removal of doubt;
the equipment of loving-kindness leads bodhisattvas to an unobstructed mind; the equipment of compassion leads bodhisattvas to tirelessness in training those to be disciplined.
The equipment of sympathetic joy leads Bodhisattvas to delighting in and finding pleasure in the garden of the Dharma;
the equipment of equanimity leads Bodhisattvas to the abandonment of attachment and aversion;
the equipment of hearing the Dharma leads Bodhisattvas to the abandonment of the hindrances.

The equipment of renunciation leads Bodhisattvas to the relinquishing of all possessions; the equipment of dwelling in the forest leads Bodhisattvas to the non-wastage of the deeds performed through roots of virtue;
the equipment of cultivating the increase of the wholesome leads Bodhisattvas to all forms of wholesomeness.
The equipment of mindfulness leads Bodhisattvas to the attainment of dhāraṇīs;
the equipment of intelligence leads Bodhisattvas to the discernment of awakening; the equipment of fortitude leads Bodhisattvas to the realization of the course of meaning.
The equipment of the foundations of mindfulness leads Bodhisattvas to the discernment of the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena;
the equipment of the right efforts leads Bodhisattvas to the cultivation and fulfillment of all wholesome dharmas.
The equipment of the bases of psychic power leads to lightness of body and mind for bodhisattvas;
the equipment of the faculties leads to the fulfillment of restraint for bodhisattvas.
The equipment of strength leads bodhisattvas to the crushing of all afflictions;
the equipment of the factors of enlightenment leads bodhisattvas to the realization of the intrinsic nature of phenomena;
the equipment of the six means of conversion leads bodhisattvas to the purification of sentient beings who are to be disciplined.
“O young men, this is the gateway to the Dharma for crossing over saṃsāra, called ‘The Compendium of the Gateway of Purification through Accumulation.
He said: “The Blessed One has taught that the accumulation of generosity leads to great wealth and a large retinue, while ethical discipline leads to rebirth in the heavens.”
“It has been heard that the cultivation of a life of faith was taught by the Blessed One for the sake of attaining great wisdom and for the purpose of crossing over one’s own saṃsāra.
The chaplain said, “Those young brahmins who, being delighted by saṃsāra, give gifts...”
It is exactly as you have said.
Young man, those sons of good family or daughters of good family who have set out upon the path to awakening should give gifts with a mind of self-restraint,
and they should maintain ethical discipline with a mind of tranquility.
Learning should be sought with a mind free from turbidity;
cultivation should be practiced for the sake of a mind of great compassion; and the remainder [should be understood accordingly].
"O young men, dharmas must be sought for the sake of fully accomplishing the equipment of wisdom, knowledge, and skillful means. This is the path to awakening;
by such equipment, awakening is attained."
Such is the cultivation, such is the mindfulness, and such, young man, is the practice of the path to awakening.
"O young men, generate the aspiration for awakening!
O young men, the path to awakening is pure through one's intention; when a vow is made, it is fulfilled.
O young men, the path to awakening is serene through the purity of one's intention."
Young men, the path to awakening is straightforward because it flows with a purity free from deceit;
young men, the path to awakening is security and well-being, culminating in unsurpassed nirvāṇa.
Make your vow!
“Choose a Buddha-field’s array of qualities, whether pure or impure, according to your wish.
Then, noble son, the young brahmin Jyotīṣka placed his right knee upon the ground before the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha and said:
“Venerable Blessed One, I generate the mind set upon unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”
In this defiled buddha-field, there are beings whose passion is slight, whose hatred is slight, and whose delusion is slight; whose minds are unshakable and undisturbed;
who possess minds free from enmity; whose minds are devoid of envy and stinginess; whose minds have abandoned false views and are established in right view;
whose minds are virtuous, whose minds seek the wholesome, and whose minds are free from the paths to the lower realms.

“O Venerable Blessed One, if such a hope of mine should be fulfilled— that I may awaken to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment for those whose minds are thrice intent upon the path to heaven, who have accumulated roots of merit through the three bases of meritorious action, and whose minds are applied to the three vehicles— then let elephant-kings appear in both my hands.
As soon as these words were spoken, by the power of the Blessed One, elephant-kings appeared in both his hands, entirely white and well-established on seven limbs.

Having seen this, he said: "Go, you must fill the entire expanse of the sky over this whole buddhafield with rain possessing eight qualities and supreme fragrance, awakening all sentient beings from this buddhafield.
May the five hindrances be abandoned by those sentient beings upon whose bodies a drop of that rain falls, or who smell its fragrance."
"Namely: may the hindrance of sensual desire be abandoned; may the hindrances of ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt be abandoned.
As soon as these words were spoken, the nāgas proceeded through the air above with such great speed.
Just as a strong man might contract his outstretched arm or extend his contracted arm,
even so those elephant-lords, having accomplished their task, turned back as previously described and stood before him.
Then, noble son, the young brahmin Jyotīṣka was filled with supreme joy.

The Tathāgata Ratnagarbha said to him: "Son of good family, when the future time has arrived, in the second incalculable eon equal to the sands of the river Gaṅgā, during the aeon named Ratnaprabhāsa, there will be a buddha-field called Ratnasañcaya.
In this world-system of four continents, you will become the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Ratnacchatrābhyudgataraśmi, up to being a Buddha, a Blessed One."
Then, noble son, the bodhisattva Jyotikṣabha prostrated his head at the feet of the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha with the fivefold limb-gesture.
The Tathāgata Ratnagarbha said: "Arise, O stainless and pure being! You have prophesied [the enlightenment] for many millions of beings."
"You shall become one whose path is supremely pure; for the sake of awakening, you shall become a supreme Victor, a leader of beings."
...and so on, up to a thousand young men and thirty million young men who had made a vow for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment in this buddha-field;
and all of them were prophesied by the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha.
As far as Vipaśyin, Śikhin, and Viśvabhū— the last of the Buddhas— were concerned,
all those young brahmin students were prophesied.
Among those brahmins who were reciters of the thousand Vedas, there was one who was the eldest and highly esteemed as a teacher, named Vāyuviṣṇu.
He said, "Furthermore, may I touch unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment in a Buddha-field of the five corruptions;
may I teach the Dharma to sentient beings who possess intense passion, intense hatred, and intense delusion.
[There was] a young brahmin named Jyotipāla.
He asked, "O Preceptor Vāyuviṣṇu, perceiving what purpose does he make his vow for a Buddha-field of five corruptions?
The Purohita replied, "A Bodhisattva endowed with complete great compassion attains awakening in a Buddha-field of five corruptions;
there he acts for the benefit of beings who are without protection, without refuge, afflicted by the defilements, and fallen into the calamity of wrong views."
It becomes a protection and a final refuge;
it delivers sentient beings from the ocean of birth;
and it establishes sentient beings in right view.
He satisfies sentient beings with the nectar-essence of nirvāṇa;
this is seen as the great compassion of a bodhisattva who makes a vow for a buddha-field in the five corruptions.
(KpSū 194)

The Tathāgata Ratnagarbha said: "O Vāyuviṣṇu, after an incalculable number of aeons equal to the sands of one Ganges River has passed, and when a second incalculable number of aeons equal to the sands of the Ganges River remains, you shall appear in the eastern direction, having traversed as many Buddha-fields as there are atoms in a Buddha-field.
There, a world-system named Kaṣāyadhvaja shall come into being."
"In that place, O virtuous man, you shall attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening;
you shall become a Tathāgata named Śālendrarāja, up to being a Buddha, a Blessed One.
Vāyuviṣṇu said: "If, O Venerable Blessed One, such a wish of mine may be fulfilled—that when I [attain] the Blessed One..."
“I prostrate at your feet with the fivefold contact; may the Blessed One then place both his feet, adorned with the sixty marks of merit, upon my head.
When, noble son, the youth Vāyuviṣṇu bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, then the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha placed both feet upon the head of the bodhisattva Vāyuviṣṇu.
Having established him, he said:
"Arise, O you whose intent is compassion and whose wisdom is sharp! Practice the conduct for the sake of supreme enlightenment.
Cut through the firm bonds of the afflictions with your steadfastness; you shall become a Buddha, benevolent and compassionate."

(KpSū 195) Then, noble son, the young brahmin Jyotipāla, having placed his right knee upon the ground before the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha, said: "Venerable Blessed One, I generate the mind directed toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment."

In this buddha-field, among beings whose minds are characterized by passion, hatred, and delusion, whose dispositions regarding the wholesome and unwholesome are unstable, and whose lifespan is forty thousand years, the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha declared: "After incalculable eons, equal in number to the sands of one Ganges River, have passed, there will remain a second [eon] during which this world-system shall be named Sahā.
For what reason is it called 'Sahā'?"
"Those beings endure passion, they endure hatred, they endure delusion, and they endure the bonds of the afflictions; for that reason, this world-system is called Sahā.
In that Sahā world-system, there will be a great eon named Bhadraka."
For what reason is he called Bhadraka?

Because in the great eon Bhadraka, there will arise one thousand Buddhas, Blessed Ones, who are Greatly Compassionate, for the sake of sentient beings whose conduct is dominated by passion, hatred, and delusion.
You, too, O noble being, have entered this great eon Bhadraka, when the lifespan is forty thousand years.

Among all beings, you shall first awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment; you shall become the Tathāgata named Krakutsanda, a Buddha, a Blessed One, who will teach the Dharma by means of the three vehicles and deliver countless beings who are being swept away by the river of saṃsāra.
"And you shall establish them on the further shore of nirvāṇa.
Then, noble son, the bodhisattva Jyotipāla prostrated his head at the feet of the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha with the five-fold salutation and stood to one side.
Then, noble son, a second young brahmin named Tumburu sat down in front of the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha.
“Venerable Blessed One, may I become a Buddha in the world during the succession of the Tathāgata Krakucchanda, when the lifespan of beings is thirty thousand years.

The Tathāgata Ratnagarbha said: “Young man, after one incalculable aeon, equal to the sands of the river Gaṅgā, has passed, and when the second incalculable aeon, equal to the sands of the river Gaṅgā, remains, you shall enter the Sahā buddha-field.”
“In the Bhadrakalpa, following the succession of the Tathāgata Krakucchanda, when the lifespan of beings is thirty thousand years,
you shall become a Tathāgata named Kanakamuni— an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha, whose fame shall resound throughout the world.
Having heard this prophecy from the Blessed One, he—
Having bowed his head at the feet of the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha and circumambulated him, he stood facing the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha;
scattering flowers over the body of the Blessed One with palms joined in reverence, he praised the Blessed One with these verses:
“Your speech is well-composed, most joyful, and exceedingly sweet; it is unerring, undisturbed, stainless, and pure.”
O supreme sage, you who possess profound intent, transcendent conduct, and surpassing wisdom; O bull among men, O best of sages, may you blaze forth!
O best of sages, you are a giver of many virtues, filled with hundreds of qualities, and a bringer of happiness to men and gods who bow before you.
Indeed, no other being exists equal to you in the three worlds; today, many beings have been prophesied by you on the path to enlightenment.

Then, noble son, the young brahmin named Viśvagupta, having placed a throne made of the seven precious gems before the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha, and having arranged upon that throne a seat worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold], set out a golden vessel; he then offered to the community of monks headed by the Buddha a golden water-pitcher filled with the seven precious gems and a staff made of the seven precious gems.

He said, "Venerable Blessed One, in a future time, when one incalculable eon equal to the sands of one Ganges River has passed and the second remains, during that Fortunate Aeon (Bhadrakalpa), while the lifespan is declining and the signs of the Kali Yuga have arisen, I shall become a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, perfected in knowledge and conduct, for those who are overwhelmed by intense passion, hatred, delusion, pride, envy, and avarice."

“May I awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment when sentient beings— who rely upon wrong views and evil friends, whose minds are obsessed with unwholesome roots, whose minds have fallen away from wholesome roots, whose minds are devoid of right view, and whose minds are unwholesome due to wrong livelihood— live for twenty thousand years in a world that is blind and leaderless, after the Tathāgata Kanakamuni has entered parinirvāṇa and the True Dharma has disappeared.”
To that brahmin Viśvagupta, O son of good family, the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha said: "Excellent, excellent, brahmin! You are a great scholar endowed with wisdom.
You, a true person, have made this vow when the signs of the Kali age had arisen, during the time of twenty thousand years of human life, in a world that was blind and without a leader."

Therefore, O noble son, let your name be Vidvagañjakaruṇāśraya (The Refuge of Compassion that Delights the Wise). In the future, after an interval equal to the sands of one Ganges River has passed, during the second remaining eon of the Bhadrakalpa, when the lifespan of beings is twenty thousand years, you will appear in this Sahā world-system.
“You shall become a Tathāgata named Kāśyapa, up to and including a Buddha, a Blessed One.
Then, noble son, the bodhisattva Vidvagañjakaruṇāśraya bowed his head at the feet of the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha with the fivefold prostration and stood to one side;
he scattered flowers, garlands, perfumes, and powders over the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha.
And praising him with these verses:
"O Best of Men, benefactor, source of delight, progenitor, you whose face is smiling, who are joyful and possess most sweet speech!"

Skilled in the knowledge of the [right] places, acting for the benefit [of beings], the most excellent holder of the ten powers, who have reached the perfection of wisdom, meditation, and liberation— homage be to you, O Sugata!
"O you whose conduct was practiced through many modes of life, whose faces are radiant, and who were prophesied for incomparable awakening—
you, the Sugatas, the best of men, along with many millions of Bodhisattvas, we pay homage to you! Thus it is said.
(KpSū 200) Then, noble son, the brahmin Samudrareṇu exhorted the fourth young brahmin, Vimalavaiśāyana.
Then, noble son, the young brahmin Vimalavaiśāyana, standing before the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha, said: "In this very same auspicious eon, I too desire awakening."

And it is not only in such a form during the Kali age; for instance, when the Tathāgata Kāśyapa had passed into parinirvāṇa and the lifespan of beings was ten thousand years, there were sentient beings whose intentions regarding generosity and self-restraint were exhausted, who were devoid of the seven riches, and whose minds perceived evil friends as teachers.
They have no interest in the three bases of meritorious action;
they are devoid of the three types of good conduct and are intent upon the three types of misconduct; their minds are agitated by the darkness of the afflictions;
and they have no interest in the three vehicles. At that time, it is impossible for anyone to accomplish the practice of awakening.
How much more so during the [aeon] of a thousand-year lifespan? Until those beings have a lifespan of only one hundred years,
at that time there is not even the name of a root of merit among sentient beings.
How much more so for those practicing the roots of virtue! Even when the world is declining in the five corruptions and the lifespan reaches ten years,
and when the intermediate aeon of weapons has arrived, at that time I shall descend from the heavens and rescue sentient beings.
Having abandoned what is unwholesome, I would establish beings in the wholesome;
indeed, I would establish beings in the ten wholesome paths of action,
and I would purify the afflictions of beings by means of those wholesome paths of action.
May I transcend the five corruptions;

and when the lifespan of beings reaches eighty thousand years, may I awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and teach the Dharma to sentient beings whose passion, hatred, and delusion are slight, and who are free from ignorance, envy, and stinginess.
"And may I establish them in the three vehicles.
O Blessed One, if such a wish of mine should be fulfilled, then may the Blessed One, Venerable Sir, grant me the prophecy of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Venerable Blessed One, as long as I do not receive such a prophecy,"
“I do not aspire to the stage of a śrāvaka, nor to the stage of a pratyekabuddha, by means of which vehicle I might be swiftly liberated from saṃsāra.
The Tathāgata Ratnagarbha said: “O Brāhmaṇa, there are these four grounds of indolence for bodhisattvas:”

Endowed with which four types of usurious assets do certain bodhisattvas experience sufferings within the prison of cyclic existence, falling into the precipice of wrong views and remaining for a long time in saṃsāra,
and do not swiftly attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening?
What are these four?
In this case, a certain bodhisattva may be of inferior conduct, have inferior companions,
and practice inferior renunciation.
Having inferior aspirations.
And how does a bodhisattva become one of inferior conduct? In this case, a certain individual is of immoral character.
He conducts himself unrestrainedly in body, speech, and mind;
he associates with those belonging to the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas;
and he is neither one who renounces everything nor one who renounces everything everywhere.
One who gives gifts while desiring the glory and happiness of gods and humans,
yet does not embrace the array of qualities of a Buddha-field through resolute intention; and one who embraces a vow without regard for those to be converted—
endowed with these four factors, a lazy bodhisattva experiences suffering for a long time in the prison of saṃsāra.
Nor does one swiftly attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Endowed with four qualities, a bodhisattva swiftly awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
What are these four?
He is virtuous, conducting himself with restraint in body, speech, and mind;
he associates and moves in the company of those who have set out in the Mahāyāna;
he is one who renounces everything, renouncing all things everywhere, and for the sake of liberating sentient beings from suffering, he gives rise to a mind of compassion.
With resolute intention, having considered the array of qualities of the Buddha-field and those to be trained, he takes up his vow.
Endowed with these four dharmas, a bodhisattva swiftly awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
These four dharmas provide support for the bodhisattva path.
Which four?
Diligence in the perfections,
and the application of the means of attracting beings.
The perfection of the divine abodes and the playful mastery of the superknowledges;
by means of four qualities, a bodhisattva should dwell without satiety.

One should dwell with insatiability regarding giving, insatiability regarding hearing the Dharma, insatiability regarding meditative cultivation, and insatiability regarding the means of attraction toward sentient beings.
These four inexhaustible treasuries must be fulfilled by a bodhisattva.
What are the four?
A Bodhisattva should fulfill the inexhaustible treasure of faith;
he should fulfill the inexhaustible treasure of teaching the Dharma, dedicating merit, and caring for destitute sentient beings.
These four are the purifications of a Bodhisattva.
Which four? Purity of ethical discipline through selflessness;
purity of meditative concentration through the absence of a sentient being;
Through the absence of a life-principle (*nirjīvatā*), there is the purification of wisdom;
through the absence of a person (*niṣpudgalatā*), there is the purification of liberation, and through the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimuktijñānadarśana*).
Four qualities are to be fulfilled by a bodhisattva. (KpSū 204)
By means of these, bodhisattvas swiftly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
they set in motion the wheel of space, the inconceivable wheel, the incomparable wheel, the ineffable wheel, the wheel of deliverance, the wheel of penetration, and the wheel of non-occurrence.

Vimalavaiśāyana, in a future time, after incalculable eons as numerous as the sands of one Ganges River have passed, when the Fortunate Eon has recently begun, during the period of the five corruptions that has subsided and the lifespan of beings is increasing to eighty thousand years, you will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.

“You shall become a Tathāgata named Maitreya, even unto a Buddha, a Blessed One. Then the brahmin Vimalavaiśāyana, having prostrated at the feet of the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha with the fivefold circle (pañca-maṇḍala), stood to one side and, intent on honoring the Blessed One with flower garlands and powders,
praised him with verses:
“O Protector, may you have a broad forehead with a beautiful, snow-white *ūrṇā*,
resembling the peak of the Golden Mountain;
O Sage, Bull among Men, Lamp of the World, filled with hundreds of virtues, who would not take refuge in you?”
"This is my time; it has been said that [I am] born in the world of Buddhas."
(KpSū 205) All one thousand Vedic scholars were incited by the brahmin Samudrareṇu, the domestic priest, toward awakening;
just as Krakutsanda, Kanakamuni, Kāśyapa, and Maitreya were prophesied, so too were Siṃha, Pradyota, and the rest, with the exception of two.
A thousand young brahmins who were reciters of the Vedas made a vow for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment during this very Fortunate Aeon;
all of them were established by the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha in unexcelled, perfect enlightenment within this same Fortunate Aeon.
The youngest among them was urged by the family priest:
"O you who possess great strength and speed, why do you gaze so long?
Generate great compassion for all sentient beings!"
And he makes his request with these verses:
“Those beings who, terrified by old age, sickness, and death, have fallen into the river of craving;
(KpSū 206)
Cast into the prison of existence, men dwell in terror within the aggregates;
having drunk the poison of the afflictions, they stand in an ocean of suffering, killing one another.
Wandering in the blind darkness of delusion where the path is lost, they revolve in the machine of impure saṃsāra.
Entirely enmeshed by suffering throughout the three realms of existence, beings abide in false views;
all living creatures wander through the five destinies like a turning wheel.
Deprived of the eye of Dharma, remember those beings who are without protection within these five destinies.
Having abandoned doubt and indecision regarding existence through wisdom, generate the aspiration for enlightenment;
become the dispeller of craving and sorrow for the world, and be a kinsman to sentient beings.
(KpSū 207)
I bow my mind for the sake of liberating the world from the bonds of affliction and for its awakening; O Supreme One, grant the eye of Dharma to those devoid of it and the path that removes delusion.
Quench with the essence of Dharma those who are burning within the prison of cyclic existence.
O Sage, having approached quickly and prostrated at the feet of the Benefactor, you should declare all your vows: "May you become a Buddha, a firm and praiseworthy leader;
may you be one who brings relief to sentient beings and delivers the world from the ocean of existence."
May you be one who bestows the faculties, the powers, and the factors of enlightenment, leading others upon the path to liberation;
release the rain of Dharma, O Cloud of Dharma, and pacify the suffering of sentient beings.
And that young brahmin Mahābalavegadhārī said,
"O Preceptor, I do not desire the splendor of those who delight in saṃsāra, nor do I have any longing for the vehicles of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas."
"I desire the unsurpassed vehicle.
Wait a moment, O Upādhyāya;
listen as I roar the lion’s roar."

Then, noble son, the brahmin Samudrareṇu, having gone forth from there, addressed his five brahmin sons who were his attendants, saying: "O children, generate the mind set upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. They also said: [We shall do so].
“We have nothing whatsoever that we might offer to the community of monks headed by the Buddha.
Furthermore, how can we, who have not yet planted roots of merit, give rise to the thought of awakening?
Then, noble son, the brahmin Samudrareṇu, the chief domestic priest, gave his first attendant, named Karabhuja, an ear-ornament made of the seven precious gems.
The second attendant, named Sthālabhuj, he gave a second earring made of the seven precious gems; the third attendant, named Jalabhuj, he gave a seat made of the seven precious gems;
and the fourth was Vegabhuj.
The attendant named Nāma gave him a staff made of the seven precious gems;
the fifth attendant, named Sārabhuj, having given him a water-pitcher made entirely of gold, said:
"Go, young men, and after presenting these items to the community of monks headed by the Buddha, generate the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment."
Then those five attendants went into the presence of the Blessed One; having presented those objects exactly as they had been deposited to the community of monks headed by the Buddha, they said:
"May the Blessed One grant us a prophecy regarding unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, so that in this auspicious aeon we may fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment."
[The usual formula applies. O son of good family, the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha has prophesied that the young brahmin Karabhuja shall become the Tathāgata named Dṛḍhasvara in the Bhadrakalpa;
after him, Sthālabhuja shall become the Tathāgata named Sukhendriyamati;
and immediately following him, Jalabhuja shall become the Tathāgata named Sārthavādin.
Following that succession, there will be a Tathāgata named Priyaprasanna;

following that succession, the young brahmin named Sārabhuja will become a Tathāgata named Haripatracūḍa. Immediately after those five young brahmins of the Bhadra-kalpa had been thus prophesied, the domestic priest spoke again to Mahābalavegadhārin: "Mahābalavegadhārin, take hold of the magnificent arrays of qualities of a Buddha-field!"
Make a vow before the Blessed One for whatever you desire;
invite all sentient beings with the flavor of the Dharma,
and practice your own conduct of awakening with firm vigor.
"Do not look at him for long anymore.
Having seized him by the arm, he brought him into the presence of the Blessed One.

Then that young man of noble family, possessing great strength and speed, sat down before the Blessed One and said: "O Blessed One, how many suns of sages will there be in this Fortunate Aeon in the future?"
The Tathāgata Ratnagarbha said: “In that auspicious aeon, O young brahmin, there shall arise fourteen hundred suns of sages.

The young brahmin asked: “Venerable Blessed One, how many of those sun-like Jinas who have entered parinirvāṇa during that great auspicious aeon will there be, until the last one, the young brahmin named Sārabhuja, who will attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment and become the Tathāgata named Haripatracūḍa?”

For that long I shall practice the conduct of a bodhisattva, accumulating the equipment of various vows, austerities, giving, self-control, restraint, learning, vigor, patience, gentleness, merit, and wisdom;
and I shall offer the first alms-food to all those of the Fortunate Aeon who have recently attained perfect awakening,
and I shall perform worship of the relics of those who have entered final nirvana.
And may I become a bearer of their true Dharma;

may I encourage, lead, and establish beings who lack ethical discipline in the perfection of ethical discipline; and may I encourage, lead, and establish beings who lack right view and have fallen into distress in right view.
May I establish those who lack such an intention in the right intention; may I establish those who lack such conduct in right conduct;
and may I demonstrate the practice of virtue to beings of various kinds.

And when the true Dharma of those Blessed Buddhas has not long since passed away, may I again kindle in the world the guidance of the true Dharma, the upholding of the true Dharma, the arising of the true Dharma, and the lamp of the true Dharma.
During the time of the intermediate aeon of weapons, may I establish sentient beings in the abstention from taking life, up to right view.
Having rescued sentient beings from the ten unwholesome paths of action and from the wrong path, may I establish them upon the right path; and may I destroy the darkness of their misconduct.
I would manifest the light of good conduct;
and for as long as there is the defilement of the eon, I would destroy the defilements of views and afflictions in the world.
At the time of the intermediate eon of famine, I would urge sentient beings toward the perfection of generosity, and so on, up to inciting and establishing them in the perfection of wisdom.
Engaging sentient beings in the six perfections, may I pacify all famines, darkness, strife, impurity, conflict, enmity, discord, and disputes;
may I extinguish the fire of the afflictions within the continuum of sentient beings.
And during the time of the intermediate kalpa of disease, may I encourage sentient beings toward the six means of crossing over.
I would engage them in and establish them in the four means of attraction;
I would shatter the darkness of disease for sentient beings,
and even pacify the afflictions within the continuums of sentient beings.

In the Sahā Buddha-field, throughout the Bhadrakalpa, may I liberate all sentient beings from such calamities as these. When the one thousand and four Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, have appeared and passed into nirvāṇa during this great Bhadrakalpa, and when the guidance of the True Dharma has entirely disappeared in every respect;
Thereafter, may I fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.

May my lifespan, once I have attained awakening, be as long as the lifespan of all the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the four thousand and four Bhadrakalpas; and may my single assembly of disciples be equal in number to the assembly of disciples of all those [Buddhas]. (KpSū 213)
And for as many beings as those four thousand Buddhas might discipline over the course of those eons, for that many beings I would discipline. Furthermore,

those who might stumble in the training of the disciples of those Blessed Buddhas, or fall into the precipice of wrong views, or harbor a mind lacking respect or a corrupt mind in the presence of those Blessed Buddhas— [I would discipline them].
May they have wavering minds regarding the Dharma and the Saṅgha;

may they harbor thoughts of lust, revile the noble ones, and commit the deeds of immediate retribution. Yet, once I have attained awakening, may I rescue them all from the mire of saṃsāra and lead them into the fearless city, the citadel of nirvāṇa.
Until the true Dharma of me, having entered final nirvāṇa, has come to an end, may I remain inexhaustible throughout this Fortunate Great Aeon (*bhadrakamahākalpa*).
When my true Dharma has reached its conclusion and the Fortunate Aeon has ended,
may those relics of mine, which constitute my birth-body, abide as immeasurable and incalculable forms of the Tathāgata, their bodies adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man.
Each individual mark would be adorned with eighty secondary characteristics.

And those forms of the Tathāgata, having gone to immeasurable, incalculable, and empty Buddha-fields in the ten directions, each single form of a Buddha would inspire, establish, and settle immeasurable and incalculable beings in the three vehicles.

In whichever Buddha-field there might be no destruction during the intermediate kalpa, there the form of the Tathāgata would protect sentient beings, just as previously described; and subsequently, a wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi) would appear.
To those Buddha-fields where sentient beings might be devoid of jewels, they would go to those Buddha-fields, rain down a shower of jewels, and manifest hidden treasures (nidhi).

And in those buddha-fields where sentient beings might be devoid of virtuous actions and afflicted by diseases, may a rain of *gośīrṣa*, *uragasāra*, and *kālānusāri* sandalwood incense fall upon those buddha-fields;
and may that rain of incense pacify the diseases of the afflictions (*kleśa*), the diseases of [wrong] views, and the diseases of the body for those sentient beings;
thereafter, may those sentient beings become devoted to the bases of meritorious action and have heaven as their ultimate goal.
“Venerable Blessed One, while practicing the conduct of awakening in such a manner, may I rescue sentient beings.
Having attained awakening, may I perform such Buddha-activity;
and even after my final nirvana, may I rescue sentient beings from infinite and boundless Buddha-fields.”

"Venerable Blessed One, if such a hope of mine were not fulfilled, and if I were not to become a medicine for sentient beings, then the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones— who reside, remain, and maintain themselves in the infinite and boundless world-systems in the ten directions— would be deceived by me; may the Blessed One therefore not grant me the prophecy of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening."
Blessed One, may I never fail those many millions of beings who have correctly entered and been prophesied for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment,

and may I never please them; and as I wander through saṃsāra for the sake of awakening, may the sound of "Buddha," the sound of "Dharma," the sound of "Saṅgha," the sound of "wholesome," and the sound of "the performance of wholesome deeds" never again fall upon my path of hearing.
“O Blessed One, may I remain forever included within the Avīci hell if such a wish of mine is not fulfilled.
Then the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha gave his approval to the young brahmin Mahābalavegadhārī.
“Excellent, excellent, O noble son! You, noble son, shall become a medicine for sentient beings and a liberator from sufferings; therefore, noble son, be known by the name Bhaiṣajyarājajyotirvimala.
In the future, you shall be Bhaiṣajyarājajyotirvimala.”

"When one incalculable aeon, equal to the sands of the river Ganges, has passed and a second incalculable aeon, equal to the sands of the river Ganges, has begun— the Bhadrakalpa— you shall offer alms-food to four thousand and four Buddhas who have recently attained perfect enlightenment, just as you yourself have made your vow."

When the Tathāgata Haripatracūḍabhadra has entered parinirvāṇa and his true Dharma has disappeared, you shall realize unexcelled, perfect enlightenment and become a Tathāgata named Roca, even unto a Buddha, a Blessed One. Your lifespan shall be half a kalpa.

As long as there shall be a community of disciples belonging to those one thousand and four Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa, so long shall there be a community of disciples for you alone, and you shall discipline that many beings.
Furthermore, even after you have entered parinirvāṇa, the disappearance of the True Dharma will not occur until the end of the great aeon, the destruction of the Bhadrakalpa itself.

And there shall be as many manifestations of the Buddha’s body as will pacify the disease of afflictions, the disease of views, and the disease of the body for sentient beings through a rain of fragrance in empty buddha-fields; and they shall establish sentient beings in the three bases of meritorious action, making heaven their ultimate goal.”

(KpSū 217) Then, noble son, the bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarājajyotirvimala said: "If, O Venerable Blessed One, such a wish of mine should be fulfilled, then may the Blessed One touch my head with his hand, which is adorned with the marks of a hundred merits."
"May he touch your head!
Then, noble son, the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha, having stroked the head of the bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarājajyotirvimala with his hand adorned with the marks of a hundred merits,
stood there.

Then, noble son, the bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarājajyotirvimala, joyful, elated, uplifted, and with a heart full of rapture, prostrated his head at the feet of the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha with the five-fold salutation; having stepped aside to one side, he stood there.
The brahmin Samudrareṇu, having covered him with a divine Kauśika garment, spoke.
“Excellent, excellent, O virtuous man! A beautiful vow has been made.
You need no longer attend upon me.”
"Abide in happiness alone."
Then, noble son, this thought occurred to the brahmin Samudrareṇu: "I have inspired many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of living beings toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment,
such that I see this entire assembly and observe that all these great beings have made most sublime vows."
Having taken possession of serene Buddha-fields, Vāyuviṣṇu and the other bodhisattvas have avoided the Kali age;
I, however, while the Kali age is currently prevailing, must satisfy sentient beings with the essence of the Dharma.
One must maintain firm resolve;
and with such a vow, I shall let out a lion's roar,
so that this entire assembly of bodhisattvas may be struck with wonder.
May this entire assembly, including the world of gods, gandharvas, humans, and asuras, pay homage to me with palms joined and perform worship;
may this Buddha, the Blessed One, grant me his approval and give me a prophecy;
and likewise, may those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who currently reside, live, and teach the Dharma to sentient beings in the ten directions, also [approve] my roaring of the lion’s roar.
They would give their approval,
prophesy their unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, and dispatch messengers so that this entire assembly might hear them and behold those messengers.

Furthermore, those bodhisattvas endowed with great compassion who, in a later time, should by means of their vow take up such a defiled buddha-field during the era of the Great Kali-yuga, and should rescue beings who are being swept away by the floods of afflictions in the wilderness of a famine of Dharma, and should perform the work of a Buddha— [they too shall attain it].
May they teach the Dharma to sentient beings;

and even after I have attained final nirvana, when inconceivable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of eons have passed, may immeasurable Buddhas, Blessed Ones, in immeasurable and incomparable Buddha-fields throughout the ten directions, speak my praise after I have passed into final nirvana.
They would spread my fame and renown, and in the presence of the bodhisattvas, they would proclaim the guiding principle of my vow.
And those bodhisattvas, having heard of my vow— which is empowered and permeated by compassion— would be struck with the utmost wonder.
They too would generate great compassion for sentient beings,
and then they would take up a vow of this very kind, just as I am taking it now,
and they too would awaken to enlightenment in such a defiled buddha-field.
They would rescue sentient beings who are being swept away by the four floods, discipline them by means of the three vehicles, and establish them upon the path to nirvāṇa.”
"O son of good family, having thus formulated this vow characterized by the cultivation of great compassion, the brahmin Samudrareṇu, the chief domestic priest,

adjusted his robe over one shoulder and approached the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha. At that time, moreover, hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of gods in the expanse of the sky played hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of divine musical instruments, and a rain of flowers fell."
And they proclaimed with one voice:
"Excellent, excellent, O noble being! Approach the presence of the Blessed One."
"Take up this supreme vow!
In a world agitated by afflictions, you shall bring peace; you shall extinguish the mass of suffering for sentient beings with the water of wisdom.
The entire assembly, with palms joined and facing him, spoke with one voice:
“Excellent, excellent, O noble man!
O preeminent scholar, act for our benefit by making a firm vow imbued with supreme wisdom; let us hear it.
And when the chaplain approached and placed his knees upon the ground before the Blessed One, the chaplain—
At that moment, this entire trichiliocosm— the Buddha-field known as Sarvāvatisantaraṇa— trembled, shook, quaked, vibrated, was agitated, was thoroughly agitated, was disturbed,
and was utterly disturbed; and musical instruments resounded even though they were not struck.
And all those beasts and birds uttered pleasant and melodious sounds,
and the trees shed forth flowers.
Whatever beings dwell depending upon the earth in this trichiliocosm— whether they have been inspired toward enlightenment or have not been so inspired— [all were affected by this light].
With the exception of those belonging to the realm of hungry ghosts and the world of Yama,
all beings became possessed of benevolent minds, virtuous minds, minds free from enmity, untroubled minds, minds of loving-kindness, and wondrous minds;
those beings who dwell in the heavens remained in the sky with such supremely joyful hearts.

With flowers, garlands, perfumes, musical instruments, jeweled parasols, banners, flags, and fine cloths, they were intent upon hearing the Brahmin’s aspiration and performing acts of worship, making sounds that were smooth and pleasing. Likewise, as far as the Akaniṣṭha heaven, the gods descended to Jambudvīpa and, remaining in the expanse of the sky, were intent upon hearing the Brahmin’s aspiration with divine perfumes and so forth, up to fine cloths.
For the sake of performing worship, the Brahmin, having joined his palms in reverence, praised the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha with these verses:
"You sport in meditative absorptions like Brahmā; you shine forth in form like Śakra."
You bestow wealth and grain like a king, and like the supreme jewel among sages;
you roar gently like a mountain and like a lion, yet you do not tremble, being as firm as Mount Meru;
you are not agitated like the lord of the oceans, for you carry both virtues and faults like the waters of the sea.

O Sage, you wash away all impurities like a flowing stream; you burn the forest of afflictions like fire; you are not attached anywhere like the wind; O Sage who demonstrates reality, you are like a god.
O Sage, you rain down the Dharma like a cloud; you satisfy the entire world like a shower of rain.
You crush the other sects like a lion; you release the fragrance of virtue like a flower. You speak with a sweet voice like Brahmā; you are like a physician who releases the world from suffering.
Abide with an even mind toward the world as toward a mother; you constantly favor it as a friend.
O Sage, cut down pride like a firm thunderbolt, and sever the creeper of craving like an enemy.
You ferry the world across like a boatman, and burn away the grass of ignorance like a sage-elephant.
Like the moon, he bestows cool radiance; like the sun, he awakens the lotuses of humanity;
like trees, he yields fruits of supreme excellence; and like a king of birds, he is surrounded by a multitude of sages.
(KpSū 223)
O Victorious Buddha, you are vast like the ocean; your mind is equanimous toward the world as toward grass or wood.
You contemplate all phenomena as empty as a dream, yet you follow the world like water.
O Sage, you who possess the excellent marks, you have prophesied that these beings shall attain enlightenment, for you are most compassionate.
O Being, disciplined one, for me who have practiced for infinite eons, you have prophesied my supreme and most excellent awakening.
O Great Seer of noble wisdom, you who delight in truth, you have prophesied my awakening; cut through my doubts.
You shall become a Buddha in the world, a refuge from the afflictions of this degenerate age, and you will establish hundreds of beings on the path of perfect peace.

Noble son, as soon as the brahmin Samudrareṇu, the chief domestic priest, stood after praising the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha with these verses, that entire assembly—including gods, gandharvas, and humans—uttered the cry of "Excellent! (sādhu).
The domestic priest said: "Bhadanta Bhagavān, I have inspired many millions of living beings toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

They have each taken possession of their own vast and magnificent Buddha-fields; they have taken possession of disciples who are well-disciplined, whose intentions are pure, and who have planted roots of merit.
These include the four thousand Vedic scholars, headed by Jyotipāla, whom the Tathāgata has prophesied as those belonging to the Fortunate Aeon."
Those good men also discipline those whose conduct is dominated by passion, hatred, delusion, and pride through the three vehicles. Furthermore,
they have avoided the defilements of the Kali age— the obscurations of intense afflictions— and have abandoned those who commit the immediate transgressions,
those who reject the true Dharma, those who revile the noble ones, those with wrong views, those devoid of the seven noble riches, and those who lack filial respect for their mothers.

They were ungrateful toward their fathers, lacking the qualities of a *śramaṇa* or a *brāhmaṇa*, performers of improper acts, doers of demeritorious deeds, and those who saw no fear in the next world; they possessed a perverted understanding of reality and were without a protector regarding the three types of good conduct.
Likewise, they were intent upon the splendors and riches of gods and humans, yet fully engaged in the ten types of misconduct.

They are devoid of the wholesome paths of action, abandoned by all spiritual friends, and forsaken by all the wise; cast into the prison of existence, they are carried away with the current, sinking in the river of caustic brine, mired in the mud of saṃsāra, and never free from the darkness of delusion;
they have been excluded from all virtuous deeds and cast out from all empty Buddha-fields, yet they remain possessed of their roots of merit.
At that time, in this Sahā Buddha-field during the Bhadrakalpa, when the human lifespan is ten years, people will be obstructed by wrong paths and fallen into great peril;
all these will have been abandoned and forsaken by virtuous and wise men.

At that time, in this wheel of saṃsāra which revolves within the whirlpool of existence, sentient beings were unprotected, without refuge, without a resort, and had become vessels for suffering; yet they avoided those [conditions] and instead took hold of their respective Buddha-fields—fields that were preeminent, well-disciplined, possessed of pure intentions, wherein roots of merit had been planted, where vigor was exerted, and where many services had been rendered to Buddhas.
Is it not so, venerable Blessed One?
The Tathāgata Ratnagarbha said: “It is so, brahmin;
in accordance with their intentions, sentient beings make their vows and take hold of the arrays of qualities of Buddha-fields, and it is for them that I have given my prophecy.”
The brāhmaṇa said: "Venerable Blessed One, my heart also trembles just like the leaf of a *kiṃśuka* tree; my mind is utterly dejected and my entire body is exhausted.
Venerable Blessed One, if sentient beings—who have become objects of compassion—were at that time abandoned by the bodhisattvas, cast into the darkness of the great *kali*-age, and forsaken by all."

"O Venerable Blessed One, may I also, in a future time, when one incalculable aeon equal to the sands of the Ganges River has passed and the second incalculable aeon equal to the sands of the Ganges remains, and during that Bhadraka Great Aeon, while waiting for the time when the lifespan of beings is one thousand years, not become weary of wandering in saṃsāra for so long while practicing the conduct of awakening."
And with the power of concentration, I am capable of receiving those to be trained through long-term ripening; practicing the six perfections, I receive those to be trained.
Furthermore, I have heard from the presence of the Blessed One: "The perfection of giving consists in the relinquishing of things and signs."

I shall practice such a perfection of giving that in future lives, when immeasurable beings come as supplicants, I may relinquish such gifts to them—namely, the gift of food, drink, solid food, soft food, what is to be sipped, and what is to be licked; clothing, beds, seats, shelters, and dwellings; garlands, perfumes, and ointments; medicines for the sick;

umbrellas, banners, flags, wealth, grain, elephants, horses, chariots, gold, silver, bullion, jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, crystals, coral, silver, refined gold, right-spiraling shells, and all such things. Thus, I myself [shall give].
With a mind of supreme faith and compassion, having given to sentient beings without desiring any fruit,

for the sake of maturing sentient beings and for the sake of favoring those beings who are to be trained, I shall relinquish the equipment of renunciation. Furthermore, whatever sentient beings might come as implacable beggars and request— namely, the renunciation of male and female slaves, villages, cities, kingdoms, wives, sons, daughters, hands, feet, ears, noses, eyes, tongues, skin, blood, bones, the body, life, or heads— I shall give them.

With such a form of renunciation, supremely serene and with a mind of compassion, desiring no fruit for myself, I shall give gifts to sentient beings out of pity for those to be trained. I shall practice such a perfection of giving as has never before been practiced by any sentient being, nor ever will be.
Furthermore, later on, some bodhisattva practicing the course toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment might make such renunciations as these:

"In those other births, throughout immeasurable and incalculable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons, while practicing the course toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, may I practice the perfection of generosity."
"May I establish the qualities of the conduct of renunciation for future bodhisattvas who are endowed with great compassion, [teaching them]:
'That which is the pacification of the afflictions of conflict is this perfection of ethical discipline.
Likewise, in the unsurpassed..."
And while practicing the conduct for the sake of perfect enlightenment, may I practice the continuous conduct of various vows of discipline and difficult austerities,
as previously stated:
"That which is non-negligence regarding sense objects and self-examination— this is the perfection of patience."
Cultivating such patience as previously described:

"That which is seclusion from all conditioned things, the cultivation of diligence toward all unconditioned peace, and the non-retrogression through the unsurpassed practice— this is the perfection of vigor."
“That which is the practice of emptiness in order to abandon all perversions regarding conditioned phenomena—this is the perfection of meditation.
“That which is the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena by their very nature—this is the perfection of wisdom.
That which is the conduct characterized by the force and momentum of firm enthusiasm throughout immeasurable, incalculable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons.
As previously stated,
no bodhisattva practicing the course toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment has ever practiced the perfection of wisdom with such firm force of enthusiasm and power.

Furthermore, no bodhisattva practicing the conduct for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment hereafter shall ever course in the perfection of wisdom with such firmness of enthusiasm, power, and momentum as I shall course in it.
I would establish the quality of guidance for the Bodhisattvas of the future who are endowed with great compassion.

From the first production of the thought of enlightenment, I would cause the great compassion of the Bodhisattvas of the future to persist until their unsurpassed final nirvana, so that these Bodhisattvas may attain what is marvelous; for this purpose, I would practice the non-conceptualization of renunciation.

Relying on ethical discipline, being without conceit regarding patience, without exertion in vigor, without dwelling in the meditative concentrations, and practicing non-duality in wisdom; may I, without longing for rewards, [serve] those beings who are destitute of the seven noble riches, who have abandoned all empty buddha-fields,

who commit the immediate transgressions, who reject the true Dharma, who revile the noble ones, who hold wrong views, and who have fallen into the perilous straits of the accumulation of unwholesome roots.
"For the sake of sentient beings who are being led astray on wrong paths, may I practice the perfections with intense strength, momentum, and enthusiasm.

And for the sake of each and every sentient being, in order to establish the continuity of the seeds of their roots of virtue, may I endure the painful sensations of the Avīci hell for ten great eons."
In this way, may I endure painful sensations among animals, hungry ghosts, impoverished yakṣas, and impoverished humans;

and just as I would establish the seed of the roots of virtue within the continuum of a single sentient being, so too for all sentient beings, may I accept those to be trained whose continuums are like empty fists, until the end of the eon, never being without purpose even through rebirths in divine happiness.
Except for those bound by a single birth, dwelling in the Tuṣita heaven, and those in their final existence whose time has not yet expired, as they seek the full awakening of enlightenment—
