And thus, O noble son, by that first production of the thought of awakening and by your proclamation of "Great Compassion," the Buddha-fields in world-systems as numerous as the atoms in the Buddha-fields of the ten directions have been filled with your voice; therefore, you have obtained the name "Mahākāruṇika" everywhere.

Therefore, O noble son, it is well that you further raise the banner of the guidance of the vow through the proclamation of great compassion for the sake of future Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas who are Great Compassionate Ones.
Therefore, O virtuous man,

for further incalculable eons equal to the atoms of a buddha-field, fill the world systems in the ten directions with the sound of your fame and renown, which are as numerous as the atoms of a buddha-field, so that you may inspire, establish, and settle many hundreds of thousands of nayutas of koṭis of incalculable beings in unexcelled perfect enlightenment, and bring them into the presence of the Blessed One.
They have been established as irreversible from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Some among them will, through their vow, take hold of the arrays of qualities of a buddha-field, and they shall later receive their prophecy.

All those whom you have inspired toward awakening will, hereafter, for as many incalculable eons as there are atoms in a buddha-field, attain buddhahood in other world-systems throughout the ten directions— as numerous as the atoms in a buddha-field— and having set in motion the wheel of Dharma, they will speak your praises, beginning with you.
"For this third reason, O good man, you are excellent.
Then, at that time, ninety-two koṭis of bodhisattvas spoke with one voice:
"We too, O Venerable Blessed One, would go to the buddha-field Santīraṇa, into the presence of that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ratnagarbha, in order to see him and pay homage to him."
And [he sent him] to see and pay homage to that good man, to whom the Tathāgata has dispatched a message of approval with three qualities,
and this stainless flower, radiant as the moon, has been sent.”
And that Tathāgata Ratnacandra said, "Go, noble sons, at whatever time you deem appropriate;
there, in the presence of the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha, you shall hear the Dharma discourse on the 'Teaching of the Entrance to Samādhi' and the 'Confidence in Conduct.
Then those two noble sons, Ratnaketu and Candraketu, [received] from the presence of the Tathāgata Ratnacandra the [teaching] *Candrarocavimala*...
Taking a flower, he set out for the world-system Ratnavicayā together with ninety-two koṭis of bodhisattvas.
Just as lightning [flashes], even so those two vanished from that assembly of bodhisattvas in the buddha-field Ratnavicayā and stood here in the Jambūvana grove in this buddha-field Saṃtīraṇa.

He approached the place where the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha was; having approached him and bowed his head at the feet of the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha, he performed worship with various miraculous displays of a bodhisattva.
Then, seeing the brahmin before the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha and the entire assembly of bodhisattvas standing with palms joined in reverence, [he spoke].
As they were speaking these words of praise for those two bodhisattvas, this thought occurred to them:
"This is that one endowed with great compassion, for whom the Tathāgata Ratnacandra has sent these stainless flowers, radiant as the moon."
Then those two bodhisattvas, having turned back from the presence of the Blessed One and presented a flower to the brahmin, said this to him:
"O virtuous man, this moon-like stainless flower, radiant as the moon, has been sent to you by the Tathāgata Ratnacandra; and a word of approval has also been sent to you, O virtuous man."
As previously stated, and so forth:
from immeasurable and incalculable Buddha-fields in the eastern direction, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas arrived at the Saṃtīraṇa Buddha-field;
taking flowers of the *candrarocavimalapuṣpa* variety, they sent these flowers to the brahmin.
And with three members, he sent forth a cry of "Well done," as previously described.
In this same way, in the southern direction, beyond ninety-seven hundred thousand nayutas of kotis of buddha-fields from this buddha-field—

There, in the world-system named Niryūhavijṛmbhita, in that buddha-field called Niryūhavijṛmbhita, there dwells and remains a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Siṃhavijṛmbhiteśvararāja; he teaches the Dharma, which is a pure discourse on the Mahāyāna, for pure bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
And in that assembly were two bodhisattva mahāsattvas: one named Jñānavajraketu and the second Siṃhavajraketu; those two bodhisattvas questioned the Tathāgata Siṃhavijṛmbhiteśvararāja.
He asked: "Venerable Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the condition for the manifestation of such a great earthquake in the world and such a great rain of flowers? ...
[as previously stated] ... up to the end.

[The passage continues] as before, until: from immeasurable and incalculable other buddha-fields in the southern direction, immeasurable and incalculable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of koṭis of bodhisattvas arrived at the Saṃtīraṇa buddha-field, just as was previously described.
Furthermore, at that time, to the west, beyond eighty-nine hundred thousand nayutas of koṭis of buddha-fields from this buddha-field, there [was a field] named Jayāvati.
There dwells and maintains his life the Tathāgata named Jitendriyaviśālanetra, who teaches the Dharma to the four assemblies by means of the three vehicles.
Therein were two bodhisattva mahāsattvas: one named Bhadravairocana and a second bodhisattva mahāsattva named Siṃhavijṛmbhitakāya; these two noble beings [approached] Jitendriyaviśālanetra...
They asked the Tathāgata about this matter: "From where does this great earthquake arise, and from where does this great rain of falling flowers come?"
...up to as previously described.

Now at that time, having passed beyond hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of Buddha-fields from this Buddha-field in the northern direction, there was a world-system named Jambu; there dwelt a Tathāgata named Lokeśvararāja, up to a Buddha, a Blessed One.
He taught the pure Dharma, which is discourse on the Mahāyāna, to the pure bodhisattvas who had set out in the Mahāyāna.
There were two bodhisattvas there:
one named Acalasthāvara and the second named Prajñādhara.
They questioned the Tathāgata Lokeśvararāja: "Venerable Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the condition for the appearance in the world of this great earthquake and this great rain of flowers?
[and so on, as previously stated].
Furthermore, at that time, having passed beyond ninety-eight nayutas of buddha-fields from this buddha-field in the downward direction,
there was a world-system named Vigatatamo’ndhakārā; therein dwelt and remained a Tathāgata named Vigatabhayaparyutthānaghoṣa.
He taught the Dharma to the fourfold assembly by means of the three vehicles.
In that buddha-field, there were two bodhisattva mahāsattvas: one named Arjavairocana and the second named Svargavairocana.
It was just as previously described.

Furthermore, at that time, in the direction above, beyond two hundred thousand buddha-fields from this buddha-field, there was a world-system named Saṃkusumitā; in that buddha-field Saṃkusumitā, there was [the Buddha] Prasphulitakusumavairocana.
There, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the Bhagavat, dwells and maintains himself; he teaches the Dharma to the four assemblies by means of the three vehicles.
In that buddha-field, there dwell two bodhisattva mahāsattvas.
One was named *Svaviṣayasaṃkocitaviṣaya* and the second was named *Dhāraṇīsaṃpraharṣaṇavikopita*. Those two noble beings questioned the Tathāgata Prasphullitakusumavairocana:
"Venerable Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the condition for the manifestation of such a great earthquake in the world?"
"And from whence comes this great rain of flowers?

The Tathāgata Vairocana with Blooming Flowers replied, "Noble son, two hundred thousand Buddha-fields below this Buddha-field, there is a world-system named Saṃtīraṇa; therein dwells [the Tathāgata] Ratnagarbha."
The Tathāgata named [Nāma], the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling and teaching the Dharma;

he was prophesying many millions of beings for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment while proclaiming this Dharma discourse entitled "The Array of the Sphere of the Bodhisattva’s Domain, the Field, the Vow, the Samādhi-sphere, and the Gate of Dhāraṇīs."
And there was one Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, a Greatly Compassionate One, who had made such a vow and spoken words permeated with great compassion,
bestowing upon the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas the prophecy and instruction regarding unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
In accordance with the form of the guidance of his vow that was manifested— just as many millions of bodhisattvas had made vows for a buddha-field,
and had grasped the array of qualities of a buddha-field and the beings to be trained—
that single bodhisattva, endowed with great compassion, surpassed the entire assembly and [chose] a buddha-field that was afflicted by the five degenerations and the age of strife and afflictions.

They were all embraced [by him]; even those who had committed the acts of immediate retribution, up to those who had reached the convergence of the roots of unwholesomeness and whose mental continuums were scorched, were all taken as disciples.
And that entire assembly, including the world of gods, gandharvas, asuras, and humans, [was embraced] by the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha.

Setting aside their own worship, they were intent on performing an act of worship for that Greatly Compassionate One; having prostrated with the five-fold salutation and standing with palms joined, they spoke his praises.
And that Mahāsattva sat before the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha, listening to his prophecy.
And when that Mahāsattva placed his right knee upon the ground before that Blessed One, the Blessed One then manifested a smile of such a kind that,
in world systems in the ten directions as numerous as the atoms in a Buddha-field, the great earth shook, trembled, and quaked in six ways, until a rain of flowers fell.
And from all those buddha-fields, for the sake of awakening them,
for the sake of demonstrating the conduct of the great compassionate vows of the bodhisattvas,
the bodhisattva mahāsattvas [were summoned] from world-systems as numerous as the atoms within a buddha-field, from the ten directions, so that they might assemble in that buddha-field.

And for the purpose of speaking this Dharma discourse entitled "The Exposition of the Gateways to Concentration and the Fearlessness of Conduct" for the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, that Tathāgata displayed such miraculous manifestations as these.”
And those two sons of good family, the bodhisattva mahāsattvas Svaviṣayasaṃkocitaviṣaya and Dhāraṇīsaṃpraharṣaṇavikopita, questioned that Tathāgata Prasphuṭitakusumavairocana:
"Venerable Blessed One, how long ago did that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahākāruṇika generate the mind for awakening?"

For how long has that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva of great compassion practiced the conduct of awakening, by which he has taken up this time when the world is in the age of five corruptions, amidst the fierce onset of afflictions in the Kali Yuga; and how has he taken as his disciples those whose mental continuums are scorched, who have committed the immediate transgressions, and who are possessed of all manner of unwholesome roots?”
The Tathāgata Vairocana of Blooming Flowers said: "O son of good family, at this very moment that Great Compassionate One has first resolved his mind upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

Go, sons of good family, to the world-system Santīraṇā to behold, pay homage to, and attend upon that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ratnagarbha, and [to hear] that instruction on the gateway of meditative concentration."
In order to hear the Dharma discourse on the fearlessness of conduct,
you should inquire about that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahākāruṇika in my name, and it should be said thus:
"The Tathāgata Prasphuṭitakusumavairocana asks after you."
"Good man, because you asked for it, the *candrarocavimala* flower has been sent and a cry of 'well done' is granted to you.

Furthermore, good man, by this first production of the thought of awakening and by your utterance of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), worlds as numerous as the atoms in the Buddha-fields in the ten directions have been filled with sound;
you have attained the sound of great compassion. Therefore, good man, you are truly excellent."

For the sake of the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas of the future who have set out in the Mahāyāna of great compassion, you raise the banner of the guidance of their vows through the expression of great compassion.
Therefore, O noble son, it is well that you, O noble son,

have filled the world systems of the ten directions— equal in number to the atoms of the Buddha-fields of incalculable eons past— with the sound of your fame and renown, which is as vast as the atoms of those Buddha-fields.
O virtuous man, you have exhorted, introduced, and established many hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of incalculable beings in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment,
and have brought them into the presence of the Blessed One.
And they were established in non-retrogression regarding unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.

Some, right there in the presence of the Blessed One, took hold of the magnificent arrays of qualities of Buddha-fields through their vows, and beings to be converted were covered by the rays of their own compassion.
As for those whom you have inspired toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment but who have not yet received a prophecy, [they too have been so established].
They too shall later receive their prophecy;

all of them, after an incalculable number of eons equal to the atoms within a buddha-field, shall attain buddhahood in other world-systems in the ten directions— world-systems as numerous as the atoms within a buddha-field— and turn the wheel of Dharma in accordance with the truth.
"Having set it in motion, they will speak in praise of you alone.
For this third reason, O good man, you are excellent.
Then, at that time, many tens of millions of bodhisattvas spoke thus: "Venerable Blessed One, we too would go to that buddha-field, Saṃtīraṇa."
In order to see, pay homage to, and attend upon that Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha Ratnagarbha,
and to see, pay homage to, and attend upon that True Person to whom the Tathāgata has sent his approval by means of three qualities.
"And these *candrarocavimala* flowers have been sent.
Then, O son of good family, that Tathāgata Prasphullitakusumavairocana said to them: "Go, sons of good family, at whatever time you deem appropriate.

There, sons of good family, you shall hear from the presence of the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha the Dharma discourse titled 'The Exposition on the Entranceway of the Fearlessness of Conduct' (*samavadhānamukhanirdeśacaryāvaiśāradya*)."
Then, noble son, those two bodhisattvas— Viṣayasaṃkocitaviṣaya and Dhāraṇīsaṃpraharṣaṇavikopita—

took from the presence of that Tathāgata Prasphullitakusumavairocana flowers called Candrarocavimalā and, together with many millions of bodhisattvas, set out from the buddha-field Saṃkusumita for this world.
In a single moment, they reached that buddha-field and stood in the Jambūvana grove; they then approached the presence of the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha.

At that time, the entire Saṃtīraṇa buddha-field was filled in this manner with Mahāyāna bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddha-vehicle practitioners, śrāvaka-vehicle practitioners, noble sons, and devas, and so forth.
With the mahoragas, it was just as if a grove of sugarcane, or a grove of reeds, or a grove of sesame, or a grove of rice were fully grown and densely packed.

In that same way, at that time, the Buddha-field Saṃtīraṇa was completely filled and densely packed with noble sons who followed the Mahāyāna, up to and including the mahoragas; and those bodhisattvas, having bowed their heads at the feet of the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha, by the power of various meditative concentrations—

Having performed worship through the miraculous transformations of a bodhisattva before the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha, and having seen the brahmin, all those assemblies stood with palms joined, speaking his praises.
Then, this thought occurred to those bodhisattvas: (KpSū 301)
“This is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahākāruṇika, for whom the Tathāgata Prasphullitakusumavairocana has sent these *candrarocavimalā* flowers.
Then those bodhisattvas, having turned back from the presence of the Blessed One, presented those *candrarocavimalā* flowers to that brahmin and said:
“O noble sir, these *candrarocavimalā* flowers have been sent to you by the Tathāgata Prasphullitakusumavairocana.”
And that cry of "Well done!

was bestowed upon you by those true persons—just as previously stated, the cry of "Well done! was announced by means of three factors—and furthermore, those flowers were rained down in the empty Buddha-fields.
And various wholesome sounds filled those buddha-fields; namely,

the sound of "Buddha," the sound of "Dharma," the sound of "Saṅgha," the sound of "light," the sound of "perfections," the sound of "powers," the sound of "fearlessnesses," the sound of "superknowledges," the sound of "non-conditioning," the sound of "non-arising," and the sound of "non-ceasing."
By means of the word "peaceful," the word "tranquil," the word "serene," the word "great loving-kindness," and the word "great compassion"—
whatever beings there were in those empty buddha-fields throughout the ten directions who were illuminated by that radiance,
whether they were humans or non-humans— all those beings, some resembling Yama and some resembling water— [were all transformed].

Some resemble mountain peaks, some resemble Brahmā, some resemble Śakra, some resemble flowers, some resemble Garuḍas, some resemble lions, some resemble the sun, some resemble the moon, some resemble stars, and some resembling jackals are seen to resemble vultures.
In whatever manner those beings were seated for the hearing of the Dharma with mental attention directed toward the side of wholesome qualities, in that very manner they appeared with their bodies;
and in that same way, noble son, those beings there saw their own bodies.
And those beings perceived the body of the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha in such a manner. Furthermore, noble son,
that brahmin Samudrareṇu, the chief priest, perceived the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha seated before him upon the filaments of a thousand-petaled lotus made of the seven precious gems.
And there, noble son, all those beings— whether sitting or standing, on the earth or in the sky— each individual being saw the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha in this way:
with their whole mind they perceived, "The Tathāgata Ratnagarbha is seated right before me," and "He is teaching the Dharma specifically for my sake."
And that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ratnagarbha, O son of good family, gave his approval to the brahmin Samudrareṇu,
saying: "Excellent, excellent, O Greatly Compassionate One, O Great Brahmin!"
For beings beyond counting, you are the compassionate benefactor; you appear as a light-maker in the world.

It is just as if, O Brahmin, there were a perfected field of flowers—of various colors, various scents, various textures, various petals, various stalks, and various roots—a place containing various medicinal preparations.
Among these flowers, some shine and radiate with color and fragrance for a measure of a hundred yojanas.
Some were two hundred *yojanas* in extent, some three hundred *yojanas*, and so forth; there,
certain flowers, by their color and fragrance, outshone and illuminated as far as the entire world-system of four continents.
And those beings there who were deprived of sight, upon smelling the fragrance of the flowers, regained their eyesight;
the deaf regained their hearing,
and even those deprived of all their limbs regained all their limbs.
And those beings there who were afflicted by the four hundred and four diseases, upon smelling that fragrance, would be completely liberated from all diseases.

And those beings there who were intoxicated, insane, excessively deranged, whose minds were asleep, whose minds were distracted, or whose mindfulness was lost— upon smelling the fragrance of those flowers, they would all regain their mindfulness.

And thus, there in the center of that field of flowers, a white lotus arose, possessing a firm core made of diamond, with a stem of beryl, a hundred delicate petals of gold, filaments of emerald and *kiṃśuka* flowers, and stamens of red pearls;
it was eighty-four thousand *yojanas* in height and one hundred thousand *yojanas* in width.
And that lotus, having pervaded with its color and fragrance world-systems in the ten directions as numerous as the atoms within a buddha-field, shone brilliantly.

Furthermore, O Brahmin, those beings in those world-systems in the ten directions—as numerous as the atoms within a buddha-field—who were discordant in their elements, whose bodies were afflicted by disease, or who lacked limbs; or those who were intoxicated, heedless, or insane; or those whose sleep had destroyed their mindfulness—[all these were restored].
Upon seeing the radiance of that white lotus and smelling its fragrance, the distracted minds of those beings would be calmed, all their diseases would be pacified,
and they would regain their mindfulness. Furthermore,
for those beings in those buddha-fields who have died and passed away not long ago, whose bodies remain undisturbed, from their corpses—

When the rays of that *puṇḍarīka* lotus fall upon them, or when they are touched by its fragrance, those corpses would regain their life-faculty and rise once more; and upon seeing their friends and kinsmen, they would all enter the garden and dwell there, endowed and possessed of the five strands of sensual pleasure. Furthermore, when they pass away from there, they would be reborn in the two Brahma-abodes.
And those who might dwell there for a long time, possessing no limited lifespan, and who, having passed away from there, would not be reborn elsewhere—
just as that field of flowers is for the brahmins, so too should this assembly of the Mahāyāna be regarded.
Just as when the time for the sun’s rising has arrived, those flowers open, blossom, glow, and shine— some reaching a height of a hundred yojanas, others even up to a thousand yojanas—
and the various diseases of many beings are pacified;
even so, the Sun of the Buddha, the Tathāgata, the True Person, has arisen in the world.
Just as those flowers, having blossomed by the rays of this risen sun, shine, glow, and radiate,
so too does the pacification of disease occur for sentient beings afflicted by various ailments.

In the same way, O virtuous man, having arisen in the world, I have covered and awakened sentient beings with the rays of compassion, and I further establish them in the three bases of meritorious action.

By you as well, immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings have been encouraged, introduced, and established in unexcelled perfect enlightenment, and brought into my presence; and by those sentient beings, in my presence, their respective vows [have been made].
Buddha-fields have been established and taken up;
some completely pure Buddha-fields have been taken up, and some impure ones,
and they have been thus prophesied by me.
Those good men who have accepted from me completely pure Buddha-fields have also accepted as their own disciples beings of pure intention, who are easy to discipline and have planted roots of merit;
yet they are not called Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, nor is this the great heroic deed of a Great Man.
Furthermore, great compassion does not arise within their minds or mental factors,
nor do those bodhisattvas seek unexcelled, perfect enlightenment for the sake of compassion toward all sentient beings;
even those who take hold of a completely pure buddha-field [do so].

Those bodhisattvas have abandoned compassion who desire a buddha-field that has been shunned by those belonging to the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; such bodhisattvas have not become possessed of the intention for wholesome knowledge.

Those who have made such a vow as this: "May we awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment in a buddha-field devoid of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, free from women who are possessed of unwholesome roots, and removed from the hells, the animal realm, and the world of Yama;
and may we teach the Dharma—the pure discourse of the Mahāyāna—to those bodhisattvas who have set out in the Mahāyāna, in a place entirely devoid of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."
Having attained awakening, may I be long-lived and endure for a long time;
may I teach the Dharma for many eons to those whose intentions are pure, who are well-disciplined, and who have come together through their roots of merit.
Therefore, those bodhisattvas are not produced merely from an intention for virtuous knowledge.
He is not called a *mahāsattva*.
And that Tathāgata Ratnagarbha, O son of good family, extended his arm and emitted rays of light of various colors, many colors, and hundreds of thousands of myriad colors from his five fingers.
Those immeasurable and incalculable rays of light, having gone forth, illuminated the buddha-fields in the eastern direction;
therein is a world-system named Aṅguṣṭhā.

In that world-system Aṅguṣṭhā, there are humans with a lifespan of ten years, who are ill-favored, prone to malice and insolence, possessed of a collection of unwholesome roots, and only a thumb's length in height.
There, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Jyotīrasa will appear.
For humans whose stature is equal to that of the Kali age, that Tathāgata will be one cubit in height; for men whose size is measured by a single thumb, he will be seven thumbs tall.
And that Tathāgata remains, stays, and maintains himself, teaching the Dharma to the four assemblies by means of the three vehicles.
Then, noble son, that entire assembly beheld that buddha-field, those humans, and that Tathāgata.

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ratnagarbha said: "By this Tathāgata Jyotīrasa, after immeasurable and incalculable eons had passed, the first thought was generated for unexcelled [enlightenment]."
In the presence of the Tathāgata Ratnacchatrābhyudgatāvabhāsa,
many millions of billions of living beings were encouraged, established, and settled in unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
In accordance with the aspirations made by sentient beings in the presence of that Tathāgata,
some took up the array of qualities of a buddha-field that was pure, while others took up one that was impure and characterized by the five corruptions (*pañcakaṣāya*).
And there, by that Mahāsattva, I was encouraged and established in unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

And there, in the presence of the Tathāgata Ratnacchatrābhyudgatāvabhāsa, I made a vow for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment regarding the array of qualities of a buddha-field in an age of the five corruptions;
that Tathāgata gave me his approval and I was prophesied for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.

This very spiritual friend who encouraged us toward awakening is an exceedingly noble person, who, while the time of the current Kali Yuga with its intense five corruptions was prevailing, took hold of a defiled buddha-field.

Those who have committed the immediate transgressions, even those who have reached the culmination of the accumulation of unwholesome roots and whose mental continuums are scorched, having fallen into the perilous wilderness of the forest of *saṃsāra*—

for the sake of such beings to be converted, that true person has been embraced by a vow; and for that true person, while remaining in immeasurable and incalculable various world-systems throughout the ten directions...
The Buddha Bhagavāns, while sustaining [the world], gave their approval and sent forth [this teaching], naming it *Mahākaruṇāvairocanasaumya*.

And that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahākaruṇāvairocanasaumya, our spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) who acts for our benefit, has very recently attained perfect awakening in the world-system Aṅguṣṭhavatī, where [the beings] are the size of a thumb.

Among those men, for those very men who were the size of a thumb, that Tathāgata— who was himself the size of a cubit— turned the righteous wheel of Dharma for a population whose lifespan was ten years.

Even when he had attained enlightenment, messengers were sent from immeasurable and incalculable world-systems in the ten directions by various Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who were staying and living there, for the purpose of making offerings.

Those Buddhas, those Blessed Ones, by whom he was first inspired, established, and settled in unexcelled perfect enlightenment; by whom he was first inspired, established, and settled in the perfection of giving up to the perfection of wisdom— remembering their former debt of gratitude, those Buddhas, those Blessed Ones, have sent flowers to that Tathāgata.

Behold, O Brahmin, how those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, perform the work of a Buddha in all the Buddha-fields among beings who have long lifespans, pure intentions, and dwell in happiness; yet that Tathāgata Jyotīrasa has attained Buddhahood in such a wretched Buddha-field of the five corruptions, and with such a short lifespan, he performs an exceedingly great amount of the work of a Buddha for beings who commit the immediate transgressions and even those who have accumulated all the roots of unwholesomeness.
Without abandoning the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, he teaches the Dharma.

In just this way, O noble son, having surpassed this entire assembly of bodhisattvas, you have made a most distinguished vow; even while existing in a wretched buddha-field during the age of the five corruptions, you have taken as your disciples those beings who commit the immediate transgressions, up to those who are possessed of all manner of unwholesome roots.

Furthermore, those great beings by whom completely pure buddha-fields have been taken up— fields devoid of the animal realm and the hells, devoid of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, where sentient beings are of pure intention, well-disciplined, and have planted roots of merit, and who have taken such beings as their disciples to be trained— these beings are said to be like flowers;
they are not the great beings who are like the *puṇḍarīka* lotus, who will perform the work of a Buddha among those who are well-disciplined and have planted roots of merit.
O Brahmin, there are four grounds for indolence for bodhisattvas.
What are the four?
The vow for a completely pure buddha-field;...

The vow for the work of a Buddha for the sake of beings with purified intentions; the vow for teaching after attaining awakening regarding discourses on the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
and the vow for long life after attaining awakening.
These are the four grounds of indolence for bodhisattvas,
by which bodhisattvas are said to be like flowers, rather than being said to be like white lotuses or great beings (mahāsattvas).

For example, O Brahmin, setting aside this assembly of great bodhisattvas, there was Vāyuviṣṇu, who took hold of an impure buddha-field and accepted as his disciples beings agitated by afflictions, including certain sons of good family belonging to the Fortunate Aeon.
These are the four bases of exertion for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Which four?
The vow for an impure buddha-field; and the vow to perform the work of a buddha for sentient beings whose dispositions are impure.
The vow to teach the discourse on the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas upon attaining awakening;
and the vow that, having attained awakening through the middle way, one's lifespan shall be neither too long nor too short—
these are the four bases of exerted vigor for bodhisattva mahāsattvas.
By which those bodhisattvas are called "resembling the white lotus," and not those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are called "resembling flowers.
It is, for example, as follows: (KpSū 312)

O Brahmin, you have now become a field for the propitious prediction of countless and incalculable bodhisattvas. In the presence of the Tathāgata, the Karuṇāpuṇḍarīka has arisen through the excellence of your vow, since you have taken as your disciples those who commit the immediate transgressions and even those who have accumulated all manner of unwholesome roots; thus, you have taken hold of a Buddha-field of intense five-fold corruption. O virtuous man, by virtue of your discourse on great compassion, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, as numerous as the atoms in the Buddha-fields of the ten directions, have bestowed upon you their applause.
Messengers have been dispatched,
you have been given the name Mahākāruṇika,
and this entire assembly is intent upon performing worship for you alone.
In the future, after incalculable eons as numerous as the sands of one Ganges River have passed, when a second period of eons as numerous as the sands of the Ganges remains,
you will become [a Buddha] in this very Sahā buddha-field during the Bhadraka Kalpa, amidst a population with a lifespan of one hundred and twenty years,
in a buddha-field characterized by old age, death, and the like, a world of blindness, leaderless, and fallen into a collection of unwholesome roots on a wrong path.
For those beings who are being afflicted, who have fallen into great peril, who have committed the acts of immediate retribution, who have slandered the noble ones, who have rejected the true Dharma,

and who have incurred the root downfalls— just as previously described— you shall, in a world crowded with such beings, become a Tathāgata, endowed with knowledge and conduct, up to and including a Buddha, a Blessed One.

Having turned back the wheel of rebirth and set in motion the wheel of Dharma, and having overturned the Māras of the Lord of Power and the Māras of the afflictions, you shall fill infinite and boundless Buddha-fields in the ten directions with your voice.
Furthermore, there will be a great assembly of great Śrāvakas, namely twelve hundred and fifty monks.
In forty-five years, you will gradually fulfill such a complete Buddha-activity.
Just as the vow was made,
and just as at that time this King Amṛtaśuddha will perform the entire work of a Buddha under the name Amitāyus after immeasurable kalpas,

even so, O Mahākāruṇika, you shall in that Sahā buddha-field, during the Bhadraka Great Kalpa, when the lifespan of beings is one hundred and twenty years, [attain it] in exactly forty-five years in such a manner.
"You shall perform the entire great work of a Buddha;

you shall become a Tathāgata named Śākyamuni. And after you, O noble being, have entered final nirvana through the unsurpassed parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma shall remain for more than a thousand years."
O virtuous man, when the True Dharma has disappeared, even those relics of yours will perform such Buddha-activities within the very body of your birth, just as you yourself made your vow;
in this way, you shall guide sentient beings for a long time.
As previously stated.

At that time, there was a brahmin in the city of Kaitapura who spoke thus: "O virtuous man, throughout those various immeasurable and incalculable eons while you practice the conduct of awakening, may I always serve as your attendant, providing necessities and acting as a companion in accordance with loving-kindness; may I attend upon you."

"May I be your father when you are in your final existence; and when you have attained awakening, O noble being, may I be your foremost donor of gifts; and may you prophesy my own attainment of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening."
And there was another sea goddess there named Vinītabuddhi;
she also said: "In each and every one of those births, until my final existence, may I be the mother who gives birth to you.
And once you have attained awakening, O Mahākāruṇika, may you prophesy my own unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
The deity Varuṇacāritranakṣatra also said: “In each and every [birth], until my final existence, may I be his wet-nurse;
and when he has attained awakening, may he prophesy my own unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”
One was named Śakra Sanema,
while the other was named Śakra Pāracintī;
both of them spoke.
“O Great Compassionate One, we too [shall follow] you through all those stages until you attain awakening;
and when you have attained awakening, may we become your pair of disciples, endowed with wisdom and possessed of supernatural powers.”
Furthermore, there was a Śakra named Ācāritracaraṇasudarśayūthika, who spoke thus: "O Mahākāruṇika, may I become the son of those [beings] in each of their respective final existences.
Another mountain goddess, named Saurabhyākiṃśukā, [spoke likewise].
She also said: "O Greatly Compassionate One, may I be your wife in each and every one of those births.
And when you have attained awakening, O True Person, may you prophesy my own attainment of unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
[There was also] the lord of the asuras named Kaduścara.

He also said: "O Greatly Compassionate One, throughout those various immeasurable and incalculable eons while you, O True Person, were practicing the conduct of awakening, may I be your companion, providing for your needs and acting in accordance with your loving-kindness;

when you are in your final existence, may I be your attendant; and once you have attained awakening, O True Person, may I be one who encourages you to turn the wheel of the Dharma in accordance with the truth."
And may I make your first teaching of the Dharma fruitful;
may I drink the essence of the Dharma,
and may I attain the medicine of the deathless.
“...until, through the abandonment of all afflictions, I may attain arhatship.

[The passage continues: And there, as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, gods, nāgas, and asuras made a vow for the practice of following the Great Compassionate One and were presented as those to be converted.
And there was one among them, an Ājīvika named Saṃjñāvikaraṇabhīṣma, who said: "O Great Brahmin, I shall be your companion in providing many necessary provisions.
Throughout immeasurable eons, I shall always be your kinsman, living off the fruits of your successful conduct."

And may I constantly approach your presence for the purpose of requesting things; may I beg for beds, seats, vehicles, elephants, horses, chariots, villages, towns, cities, sons, daughters, flesh, blood, skin, bones, hands, feet, tongues, ears, noses, eyes, and heads.
O Great Brahmin, may I become such a companion to you in the perfection of giving.
"May I become a companion unto the perfection of wisdom!
O Great Brahmā, may I be such a companion to you as you practice the conduct of awakening in the six perfections; until you attain awakening, may I occupy the station of your disciple."

“May I master eighty thousand aggregates of Dharma and become a teacher of the Dharma who never falters; and may you, in turn, grant me the prophecy of my attainment of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Having heard this, noble son, the brahmin Mahākāruṇika prostrated with his head at the feet of the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha using the five-pointed salutation.
Having summoned that Ājīvika, who was formidable due to his power to alter perceptions, he said:

"Excellent, excellent, O noble man! Since you will become my companion for the unsurpassed conduct, you shall attend upon me for the purpose of begging for requisites throughout immeasurable, incalculable thousands of millions of future births."
"Then, with a serene mind, I shall give it,
so that you do not become a partaker of demerit.
Furthermore, noble son, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahākāruṇika [spoke thus] to the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha.

He spoke before [the Buddha]: "Venerable Blessed One, if, while I am practicing the conduct for unexcelled perfect enlightenment throughout those various immeasurable, incalculable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of eons, there should be beggars who stand before me and beg for food— whether with gentle words, or manly words, or overbearing words, or clear words— and they should thus entreat me;
Venerable Blessed One, if I should give rise to even a single moment of anger toward a petitioner,
or should give rise to a lack of faith; or if I should give a gift while longing for the fruit and ripening of that gift,

then may I have deceived those immeasurable and incalculable Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who reside, remain, and maintain themselves in other world-systems throughout the ten directions, and who teach the Dharma.
And may I not awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment,
O Venerable Blessed One, if I were to give a gift with a mind of faith to a petitioner.
Furthermore, may there be no misappropriation of what has been given out of faith by the recipient of the gift,
so that it does not become an obstacle through unwholesome states;
otherwise, even to the extent of the tip of a single hair, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, would be deceived by me.
If they were to create even a hindrance as small as the tip of a hair to the wholesome qualities of the recipient,
I too would go to the Avīci hell;
as it is with food, so it is with clothing.
"As long as there may be supplicants who ask for my head—
whether with gentle words, harsh words, overbearing words, or clear words— and should I, O Venerable Blessed One, give rise to even a single moment of anger toward such a supplicant,"
If I were to give rise to a thought of lack of faith,
or if, desiring the fruit and maturation of my gift, I were to abandon my head,
the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, would be deceived by me.
“May I too be destined for the Avīci hell;
as it is with generosity, so should morality, up to wisdom, or renunciation be spoken of.
(KpSū 319)
And that Tathāgata Ratnagarbha, O son of good family, gave his approval to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahākāruṇika, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, O noble person!
With a mind established in great compassion, this vow has been made by you, O noble person."
And, noble son, that entire assembly, including the world with its gods, gandharvas, humans, and asuras, stood with palms joined and uttered words of praise:
"Excellent, excellent, O virtuous man!
O virtuous man, you have made this vow with a mind established in great compassion."
"You, too, shall satisfy sentient beings with the dharmas that lead to the six destinies.
And, noble son, just as the Ajīvika bodhisattva Saṃjñāvikārabhīṣma made his vow regarding the recipient of the gift,
in that very same way, eighty-four thousand living beings made their vows.

And that noble son, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahākāruṇika, having heard such aspirations from those eighty-four thousand living beings, made a vow out of fear regarding the transformation of perceptions.
Then Mahākāruṇika, filled with supreme joy and gladness, stood with palms joined and, surveying the entire assembly, spoke with a mind of supreme delight:

“Oh, how wonderful! When the world is without a leader, during the time of a famine of the Dharma, in the great battle of afflictions, in the Kali age characterized by the five corruptions, may I become a caravan leader, a light-maker, and a lamp-bearer for those who are unprotected and blind, showing them the way.”

For it is truly wonderful that, from my very first production of the thought of awakening, I have obtained such companions for this unsurpassed conduct of awakening, who will in my future lives become recipients of my head, and who will become recipients of my eyes, ears, nose, tongue, hands, feet, skin, bones, blood, and even my food.”

Furthermore, noble son, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahākāruṇika, seated before the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha, said: "Venerable Blessed One, throughout those various immeasurable, incalculable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of koṭis of eons, in whatever successive births I may have, if beggars should approach me seeking food, or drink, or even as far as my head, let them receive it— even down to the very last."

May they accept from my hand even a measure as small as the tip of a single hair, until the very end of enlightenment. If, after I have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, I were not to liberate those beings from cyclic existence,
nor were I to grant them a prophecy regarding the vehicle of the śrāvakas, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, or the Great Vehicle, [may I not attain enlightenment].
“May the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who are currently in the ten directions, be deceived by me, and may I not awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment!”
Furthermore, noble son, the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha gave his approval to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahākāruṇika:
"Excellent, excellent, O virtuous man! Such is your vow for the conduct of awakening, O virtuous man."

Just as the Tathāgata Meruśikharidhara formerly made a vow before the Tathāgata Lokeśvarajyotis at his first production of the thought of awakening, and practiced such a bodhisattva conduct exactly as that vow was made; so too [did this one].

Great eons as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā have passed since that virtuous man, in the eastern direction, in the world-system called Jvālapratisaṃkhyā within a buddha-field numbering one hundred thousand koṭis, attained unexcelled, perfect enlightenment during the time when the lifespan was one hundred years;
he became the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Bhagavat named Jñānakusumavirajasamucchrayabodhīśvara.
Having performed the work of a Buddha for forty-five years, he entered the realm of nirvana without remainder of substrate (*anupadhiśeṣe nirvāṇadhātau*).
Indeed, after that Tathāgata Mahākāruṇika Jñānakusumavirajasamucchrayabodhīśvara had passed into final nirvana, the guidance of the True Dharma (*saddharmanetrī*) remained for a thousand years;
and after the True Dharma had disappeared, the semblance of the True Dharma (*saddharmapratirūpaka*) remained for another thousand years.

O Mahākāruṇika, when the Tathāgata Jñānakusumavirajasamucchrayabodhīśvara has entered parinirvāṇa and the guide of the True Dharma remains, there may be monks or nuns who are counterfeiters of the True Dharma—those of immoral conduct, evil nature, and improper behavior; those who take possession of the property of a stūpa without shame; or those who are defiled by a lack of shame for interrupting the worship of the Dharma, whether toward the Saṅgha of the four directions or the Saṅgha present before them.

Or whether it was robes, alms-food, bedding and seats, or medicinal requisites for the sick, which had been cut off from his personal possession and either consumed by himself or given to householders—
by that Tathāgata Jñānakusumavirajasamucchrayabodhīśvara, O Mahākāruṇika, all of them were indeed successively prophesied through the three vehicles.
"O Mahākāruṇika, whoever were clothed in saffron robes within the teaching of that Blessed One, they were all prophesied to be non-retrogressive with respect to the three vehicles.

Even those monks, nuns, laymen, or laywomen who had fallen into root transgressions were previously prophesied by that Tathāgata— by virtue of the ripening of the roots of merit from perceiving him as the Teacher— to be non-retrogressive with respect to the three vehicles."

Furthermore, noble son, that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahākāruṇika said in the presence of the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha: "O Venerable Blessed One, this indeed is my vow: for as long as I am practicing the conduct of unsurpassed awakening, whatever sentient beings I may lead toward, inspire, and establish in the perfection of giving, up to..."
In the perfection of wisdom, I would apply even so much as the measure of the tip of a hair’s end toward a root of virtue;

and while practicing the conduct until the limit of enlightenment, if I were not to establish those beings in the stage of non-retrogression through the three vehicles— even if it were but a single being— then the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who reside, dwell, and maintain themselves, teaching the Dharma in immeasurable and incalculable world-systems in the ten directions, would be deceived by me.

May I not awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment until, O Venerable Blessed One, having attained unsurpassed knowledge, those beings who are in my teaching and clad in saffron robes—
whether they have committed a root offense, or have fallen into wrong views, or [are involved] in the three... [may I not awaken until I have purified them].

"O Blessed One, those monks, nuns, laymen, or laywomen who have stumbled regarding the Jewels and committed offenses— if they should produce toward me, for even a single moment, the perception of a Teacher or a mind of reverence, or should produce a mind of reverence toward the Dharma or the Saṅgha; if, O Venerable Blessed One, I were not to prophesy that those beings are irreversible through the three vehicles, then [I would be at fault]."
If they were to abandon even a single sentient being, the Buddha Bhagavāns would be deceivers, and may I not attain unsurpassed,
perfect, and complete awakening. Once I have attained awakening— (KpSū 324)

And, O Venerable Blessed One, may my red *kāṣāya* robe be honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by gods and humans. At the mere sight of it, may beings with the *kāṣāya* around their necks become irreversible from the three vehicles. May those beings who are oppressed by hunger and thirst, deprived of food and drink, or even those suffering the poverty of *yakṣas*, including the beings of the world of Yama, should they desire the *kāṣāya* even for as little as four finger-breadths—[may all these attain fulfillment].
May they all be endowed with food and drink and have their intentions fulfilled.
As for those beings who are full of mutual hostility and enmity, or who have entered into mutual conflict and battle— whether they be gods,
yakṣas, rākṣasas, nāgas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, kumbhāṇḍas, or piśācas— [may they likewise be so].
Or if humans who have entered into battle should call to mind the saffron robe (*kāṣāya*),

those beings would become possessed of a compassionate mind, a gentle mind, a mind free from enmity, and a pliant mind— those beings who, in the midst of battle, dispute, war, or strife, [hold] a fragment of the saffron robe for the sake of protection, worship, and reverence.
Those beings would always be invincible, unshakable, and unharmed;
they would be safely delivered from that battle, war, quarrel, or dispute.
Venerable Blessed One, if this saffron robe were not endowed with these five noble qualities, [I would not wear it].
May the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who reside in the ten directions, not be deceived by me;
until such time as I am unable to fully accomplish the entire work of a Buddha,
may the Dharmas not be lost to me, and may I not be able to win over those of other sects.

And those, O Venerable Blessed One, who shall pay homage to me from the time I have attained full awakening until my final nirvāṇa, or who shall utter the words, "Homage to Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata," [shall all attain supreme perfect awakening].
"The obscuration of all their karma will be exhausted, and in the end, they shall attain final nirvana through the unsurpassed parinirvāṇa of a Buddha.
Furthermore, O son of good family, that Tathāgata Ratnagarbha extended his right arm, stroked the head of the Bodhisattva Mahākāruṇika with the palm of his hand, and said:
“Excellent, excellent, O noble person! Your vow is virtuous and your reflection is auspicious.
In this very way, O noble person, through these five noble qualities, your dyed saffron robe shall become a means of sustenance for sentient beings.”

Furthermore, noble son, through that prophecy, by means of the joy and clarity born of his approval, and through the touch of the right hand of the Tathāgata— whose fingers were long and adorned with merit, and whose palm was soft and youthful— that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahākāruṇika,
though remaining in the state of a youth, became as if twenty years of age in terms of his physical stature.
(KpSū 326) Furthermore, noble son, that entire assembly— including gods, gandharvas, and humans— stood with palms joined,

intent upon performing an act of worship for the Greatly Compassionate One. Having offered worship to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahākāruṇika with flowers and musical instruments, they praised him with verses of various colors.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, "The Prophecy for Bodhisattvas," in the Mahāyāna sūtra *Śrīkaruṇāpuṇḍarīka*.
(KpSū 327) Chapter Five, titled "On Giving.
Furthermore, O son of good family, that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahākāruṇika [offered] to the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha...

Having prostrated at the feet [of the Buddha] with the five-fold maṇḍala and with his head, he sat down before the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha and questioned the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha: "The Blessed One has taught the Dharma discourse entitled 'The Entrance to Concentration, the Entrance to the Purification of Provisions,' which is the path for Bodhisattvas."

"To what extent, Blessed Lord, has the Blessed One taught the path for bodhisattvas—the Dharma discourse on the gateway of the purification of the equipment through the instruction on the gateways of meditative concentration?
To what extent, Blessed Lord, does this Dharma discourse on the gateway of the purification of the equipment through the instruction on the gateways of meditative concentration become complete?
Or by what kind of equipment, Blessed Lord, is a son of good family or a daughter of good family endowed so as to be firmly established?"
“In what manner is it adorned by the exposition through the gateway of meditative concentration?

Then, O noble son, that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ratnagarbha said this to the Bodhisattva Mahākāruṇika: “Excellent, excellent, Mahākāruṇika! Your question is auspicious; your eloquence is sublime.”
To an even greater degree, you have arisen as one who brings benefit and great assistance to immeasurable and incalculable bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, who are endowed with great compassion.
For it is indeed so, O Mahākāruṇika, that you consider this very question to be worthy of being asked of the Tathāgata.
Therefore, O Mahākāruṇika, listen; pay close and careful attention.

For those sons of noble family who have set out in the Mahāyāna, there is a samādhi called Śūraṅgama, the Great Compassionate One, wherein a bodhisattva established in that samādhi enters into all samādhis;
there is a samādhi called Ratnamudrā, by which all samādhis are sealed;
and there is a samādhi called Siṃhavikrīḍita, established in which one sports with all samādhis.
The samādhi called *Sucandra* illuminates all samādhis;
the *Candradhvajaketu* samādhi bears the banner of all samādhis;
and the *Sarvadharmodgata* samādhi contains all samādhis within it.
The samādhi named *Vilokitamudra* surveys the summit of all samādhis.

Abiding in the *Dharmadhātuvigata* samādhi, the bodhisattva proceeds toward the definitive determination of the entire realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). Abiding in the *Niyatadhvajaketu* samādhi, he upholds the banner of all samādhis.
Abiding in the Vajra Samādhi, one pierces through all samādhis.
Abiding in the Dharmapraveśamudrā Samādhi, one seals all phenomena.
By means of the Samādhirājasupratiṣṭhita Samādhi, one becomes established as a sovereign among all samādhis.
By means of the concentration called "Emission of Rays," rays radiate forth into all concentrations;
by means of the concentration called "Power and Vigor," one exercises power and vigor within all concentrations;
and by means of the concentration called "Emergence," one emerges above all concentrations.
By means of the concentration of the exposition of etymologies, one enters into the entry into the designations of all concentrations;
by means of the concentration of the entry into designations, one enters into the names of all concentrations;
and by means of the concentration of the surveying of the directions, one surveys all concentrations.
By means of the concentration on the differentiation of all phenomena, one enters into the state of differentiation of all phenomena;
by means of the concentration on the seal of retention, one maintains the seals of all concentrations;
by means of the concentration on the seclusion of all phenomena, one enters into the nature of seclusion within all concentrations.
By means of the concentration of non-forgetfulness, all concentrations are not forgotten.
By means of the concentration immovable in all phenomena, one abides in the state of being immovable within all concentrations.
[This is] the ocean-seal of the convergence of all phenomena.
In the Samādhi [of the Name], all samādhis reach a state of inclusion and convergence.
In the Samādhi of Non-conceptualization regarding All Phenomena, all samādhis reach a state of non-conceptualization regarding arising and passing away.
By means of the Samādhi of Pervading Space, all samādhis pervade space.
By means of the samādhi of the non-interruption of all phenomena, all samādhis proceed without interruption.
By means of the samādhi of the vajra-maṇḍala, one maintains the maṇḍala of all samādhis.
By means of the samādhi of the single flavor of all phenomena, one maintains the flavor of all samādhis.
By the *raṇajaha* concentration, one abandons all afflictions that serve as equipment for conflict.
By the *sarvadharmānutpāda* concentration, one demonstrates the non-arising and non-ceasing of all phenomena.
By the *vairocana* concentration, one cultivates, heats, and illuminates all concentrations.

By means of the concentration of the non-extinction of all phenomena, one discerns all concentrations. By means of the unblinking concentration, the dharmas of concentration are never sought within any concentrations.
By means of the homeless concentration, [one does not dwell] at any time within any concentrations. (KpSū 331)
He perceives the stability of phenomena (*dharmasthiti*).
By means of the space-like concentration (*gaganakalpa-samādhi*), he perceives all concentrations as having the nature of space and being without essence.
By means of the mindless concentration (*niścitta-samādhi*), the mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitasika-dharma*) within all concentrations are abandoned.
By means of the concentration of the boundlessness of form, one illuminates form;
by means of the concentration of the stainless lamp, one acts as a lamp for all concentrations;
by means of the concentration of the boundlessness of all phenomena, one displays boundless knowledge within all concentrations.
By means of the lightning-flash samādhi, he displays knowledge that is limitless within all samādhis.
By means of the illuminating samādhi, he demonstrates the gateway of illumination within all samādhis.
By means of the samādhi that reaches the limits of the realms, he demonstrates for the purpose of making known the limitlessness of all samādhis.

By means of the concentration called *samādhi-śuddha-sāra*, one attains emptiness within the phenomena of concentration; by means of the concentration called *meru-citra*, one demonstrates the hollowness of all phenomena;
and by means of the concentration called *vimala-prabha*, one removes the impurity of all concentrations.
By means of the concentration called "Non-differentiation of All Phenomena," he demonstrates the isolation of all concentrations.
By means of the concentration called "Producer of Delight," he attains delight in all concentrations.
By means of the concentration called "Sporting with the Intrinsic Nature of All Phenomena," he demonstrates the non-apprehension of form within all concentrations.
By means of the concentration called "Transformation of Lightning," he demonstrates the absence of defining characteristics in all concentrations.
By means of the concentration called "Stainless Non-Abandonment of All Dharmas," he displays the stainless knowledge of all concentrations.
By means of the concentration called "Inexhaustibility," he demonstrates that for all concentrations there is neither exhaustion nor non-exhaustion.
By means of the samādhi of the inconceivable purity of all phenomena, he shows all phenomena to be like reflections.
By means of the samādhi possessing splendor, he kindles the fire of knowledge within all samādhis.
By means of the samādhi free from exhaustion, he shows that all samādhis do not undergo exhaustion.
By means of the immovable concentration, one does not move, tremble, or proliferate with respect to all phenomena.
By means of the increasing concentration, one perceives the objects of knowledge as they increase within all concentrations and meditative attainments.
By means of the sun-lamp concentration, one radiates the faces of light rays upon all concentrations.

By means of the moon-pure (*candravimala*) samādhi, one brings light to all samādhis. By means of the pure-reflection (*śuddhapratibhāsa*) samādhi, one attains the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) within all samādhis.
By means of the form-and-formless (*kārākāra*) samādhi, one performs the activity of dwelling in forms and perceives the banner of knowledge (*jñānaketu*).
By means of the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*), one pierces through all phenomena, yet does not perceive even the piercing itself.
By means of the concentration of mental stability (*cittasthita-samādhi*), the mind does not move, does not tremble, does not appear [as an object], and does not undergo affliction.
Nor does it occur to him, "This is mind.
By means of the Samādhi of Universal Radiance, he perceives radiance within all samādhis.
By means of the Well-Established Samādhi, he becomes established in the state of being well-established within all samādhis.
By means of the *ratnakūṭa* (Jewel-Crest) samādhi, one appears like a jewel-peak among all samādhis.
By means of the *varadharmamudrā* (Seal of the Supreme Dharma) samādhi, all samādhis are sealed;
through the equality of phenomena (*dharmasamatā*), one does not perceive any phenomenon whatsoever as being apart from equality.

By the concentration called "Relinquishing Delight," one relinquishes delight in all phenomena. By the concentration called "The Torch of Dharma," one attains that which is uncreated by Māra regarding all phenomena. By the concentration called "Free from Syllables," one does not perceive even a single syllable among all phenomena.
By means of the concentration that cuts off objective referents, one completely severs all objective referents.
By means of the concentration that is without transformation, one does not perceive any transformation among all phenomena.
By means of the concentration that is pure by nature, one does not perceive any assistance among all phenomena.

By means of the concentration called "dwelling nowhere," one does not perceive a dwelling in any phenomena. By means of the concentration called "free from cataracts," one does not observe the practice of any concentrations and transcends the realm of darkness.

By means of the concentration that has reached the accumulation of all virtues, one abandons the accumulation regarding all phenomena. By means of the concentration of abiding in mindlessness, one does not perceive "mind" in any phenomena. By means of the concentration that has reached the factors of enlightenment, one awakens to all phenomena.
By means of the concentration that transforms mindfulness, one attains incalculable eloquence regarding all phenomena.
By means of the concentration purified by the knowledge of its activity, one attains the state of being neither equal nor unequal toward all phenomena.
By the *jñānaketu-samādhi*, one transcends the entire triple world;
by the *jñānopaccheda-samādhi*, one perceives the severance of all phenomena;
by the *jñānavikaraṇa-samādhi*, one attains the state of the dispersal of all phenomena.
By means of the concentration without a basis, one perceives all phenomena as being without support. By means of the concentration of the single array, one does not perceive any duality of phenomena.
By means of the concentration possessing the production of forms, one perceives the non-production of forms of all phenomena.
By means of the samādhi that shatters the foundation of all existences through the exercise of all sovereign powers, one enters into the knowledge of penetration regarding all phenomena;
by entering into which, one does not apprehend anything at all.
By means of the samādhi that enters into conventional sounds, one enters into all conventional sounds and designations.
Through the concentration of vocal sounds free from syllables, one perceives the liberation from syllables regarding all phenomena;
through the concentration of the desire for the torch of knowledge, one shines, blazes, and radiates within all concentrations.
By means of the samādhi manifested by the characteristic of supreme knowledge, one displays the impure characteristic within all phenomena.
By means of the samādhi characterized by non-apprehension, one perceives the meaning of the lack of defining characteristics within all phenomena.
By means of the concentration endowed with the excellence of all aspects, one becomes endowed with the excellence of all aspects regarding all concentrations on phenomena.
By means of the concentration that easily abandons all suffering, one perceives non-reliance toward all phenomena.
By means of the concentration of inexhaustible causes, one does not perceive anything exhaustible among all phenomena.
By means of the concentration called "Upholding," one upholds all concentrations and all phenomena,
yet one does not perceive correctness or falsity.
By means of the concentration called "Tranquility through the Manner of Cessation," one does not perceive any compliance with or opposition to all phenomena.
He perceives thus:
by means of the concentration of stainless radiance (*vimalaprabhāsa*), he does not perceive any impurity of the conditioned within all concentrations;
by means of the concentration that follows the essence (*sārānugata*), he finds no lack of essence among all phenomena.
By means of the concentration called "Stainless Full Moon," one becomes perfected in the qualities of all concentrations.
By means of the concentration called "Great Array," one becomes endowed with the great array within all concentrations.
By means of the concentration called "Discrimination of All Worlds," one illuminates all phenomena with wisdom.
By means of the samādhi called Illumination of Equanimity, one attains one-pointedness in all samādhis;
by means of the samādhi called Freedom from Strife, one does not engage in strife regarding any phenomena;
by means of the samādhi called Dwelling Without Wind, one forms no attachment to any phenomena.
By means of the concentration of non-mind as it truly abides, suchness does not recede from all phenomena.
By means of the concentration that thoroughly crushes the defilement of body, one does not perceive a self-identity in all phenomena.
By means of the concentration that attains the sky through the destruction of the defilement of speech, (KpSū 338)
A bodhisattva does not perceive any verbal activity regarding all phenomena.
Abiding in the concentration that is unattached like space, moving with the freedom of space, and untainted, the bodhisattva attains the state of being unattached like space regarding all phenomena.
This entrance into concentration is the entry point for bodhisattvas who have set out upon the Mahāyāna.
In this regard, what is the Dharma discourse that summarizes the gateways to the purification of the accumulations for bodhisattva mahāsattvas?
The accumulation of generosity of bodhisattvas conduces to the maturation of sentient beings;
the accumulation of ethical discipline of bodhisattvas conduces to the fulfillment of their vows.
The equipment of patience leads to the fulfillment of the primary and secondary marks of Bodhisattvas;
the equipment of vigor leads to the fulfillment of all tasks of Bodhisattvas;
the equipment of meditative concentration leads to the state of having a mind like that of a well-bred horse.
The equipment of wisdom leads bodhisattvas to the full comprehension of all afflictions; the equipment of learning leads bodhisattvas to unimpeded eloquence;
the equipment of merit leads bodhisattvas to being the source of sustenance for all sentient beings.
The accumulation of knowledge leads Bodhisattvas to unimpeded knowledge;
the accumulation of tranquility leads Bodhisattvas to a pliant mind;
the accumulation of insight leads Bodhisattvas to the removal of doubt.
The equipment of loving-kindness leads Bodhisattvas to an unimpeded mind; the equipment of compassion leads Bodhisattvas to tirelessness in bringing others to maturity;
the equipment of sympathetic joy leads Bodhisattvas to delighting in and finding pleasure in the garden of the Dharma.
The equipment of equanimity leads Bodhisattvas to the abandonment of attachment and aversion;
the equipment of hearing the Dharma leads Bodhisattvas to the abandonment of concealment;
the equipment of renunciation leads Bodhisattvas to the relinquishing of all possessions.
The equipment of dwelling in the forest leads bodhisattvas to the non-wastage of actions performed;
the equipment of mindfulness leads bodhisattvas to the attainment of dhāraṇīs;
the equipment of intelligence leads bodhisattvas to the differentiation of wisdom.
The equipment of the [five] destinies serves for Bodhisattvas to awaken to the meaning of the destinies;
the equipment of the foundations of mindfulness serves for Bodhisattvas to awaken to the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena;
the equipment of the right efforts serves for Bodhisattvas to abandon all unwholesome phenomena.
And for the cultivation of all wholesome dharmas,
the equipment of the bases of psychic power leads to lightness of body and mind for bodhisattvas;
the equipment of the faculties leads to the fulfillment of the faculties of all sentient beings for bodhisattvas.

The equipment of power leads bodhisattvas to the non-overwhelming of all afflictions; the equipment of the factors of enlightenment leads bodhisattvas to the realization of the intrinsic nature of phenomena;
the equipment of the path leads bodhisattvas to the complete transcendence of all wrong paths.
The equipment of truth leads bodhisattvas to the removal of unwholesome qualities and the attainment of rebirth in the higher realms.

The equipment of the analytical knowledges leads bodhisattvas to the severing of the doubts of all sentient beings. The equipment of the reliances leads bodhisattvas to knowledge that is not dependent on others.
The accumulation of spiritual friends serves as the gateway for bodhisattvas to all virtuous qualities.
The accumulation of intention serves for bodhisattvas to never deceive any world.
The accumulation of application serves for bodhisattvas to transcend all other accumulations.
The equipment of high resolve leads Bodhisattvas to progress toward excellence;
the equipment of solitary retreat leads Bodhisattvas to the practice of the Dharma as it has been heard;
the equipment of the means of attraction leads Bodhisattvas to the maturation of sentient beings.

The equipment for upholding the true Dharma leads Bodhisattvas to the non-interruption of the lineage of the Three Jewels. The equipment consisting of skill in knowing the methods of dedication leads Bodhisattvas to the purification of the Buddha-field.
“The equipment of skill in means leads bodhisattvas to the fulfillment of the knowledge of omniscience.
Noble son, this is the Dharma discourse entitled ‘The Compendium of the Gateways to the Purification of the Equipment of Bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, noble son, the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha, having surveyed the assembly of great bodhisattvas, addressed Mahākāruṇika...
Having addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, he said: "In that regard, O Mahākāruṇika, by what kind of adornment of fearlessness is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva adorned when he fulfills patience?
For the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who perceives the ultimate truth, his mind possesses an unfailing exertion throughout the entire triple world."
He who possesses a mind free from grasping toward all sentient beings is said to have the great śramaṇa-dharma of fearlessness, whose mind regarding all phenomena is equal to space in the hand.
This, O Mahākāruṇika, is the adornment of fearlessness for a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, how does the fulfillment through patience occur? Even the slightest... (KpSū 342)
In that regard, one does not perceive any dharma that could be awakened to or fully realized; rather, one has conviction in dharmas that are without karmic maturation—
namely, both loving-kindness and selflessness,
as well as compassion and the absence of a sentient being.
Joy and being devoid of life-force, equanimity and the absence of a person;
generosity and a tamed mind,
ethical discipline and a peaceful mind.
Patience and a mind of forbearance;
vigor and a mind of seclusion; meditative concentration and a mind of profound reflection.
Wisdom and magnanimity of mind;
the application of mindfulness and a state of mind free from mental engagement;
the right exertions and a state of mind characterized by non-arising and non-cessation.
The bases of miraculous power and the state of immeasurable mind; faith and the state of unattached mind;
mindfulness and the state of self-arisen mind.
Concentration and the state of non-mindfulness upon entering meditative absorption;
the faculty of wisdom and the state of a mind beyond the senses; power and the state of an unassailable mind.
The factors of enlightenment and the state of mind that discerns awakening;
the path and the state of mind that cultivates it;
and tranquility and the state of mind that is peaceful.
Vipaśyanā and a state of mind free from delusion;

the cultivation of the noble truths and a state of mind characterized by the cultivation of ultimate thorough knowledge; and mental attention directed toward the Buddha and a state of mind that is without its own fixed form.
And the mental attention to the Dharma and the state of mind equal to the realm of phenomena;
the mental attention to the Sangha and the state of non-abiding mind;
the ripening of sentient beings and the state of a mind primordially pure.
The upholding of the true Dharma and the state of a mind undifferentiated from the dharma-realm;
the purification of the buddha-field and the state of a mind equal to space;
and the perfection of the marks and the state of a mind free from marks.
The attainment of patience and the state of a mind that does not apprehend; the stage of non-retrogression and the state of a mind that neither turns toward nor turns away;
the mind that adorns the seat of enlightenment and the state of a mind that is the mandala of the triple world.
The mind of subduing Māra and yet the state of a mind that favors all sentient beings;
awakening and the equality of all phenomena and yet the state of the mind of awakening;
the turning of the wheel of Dharma and yet the state of a mind in which no phenomena are turned.
The manifestation of the great parinirvāṇa and the state of mind that realizes the intrinsic nature of saṃsāra.”

While this Dharma discourse was being spoken, sixty-four hundred thousand bodhisattvas from the ten directions [attained] the teaching on the gateway of the application of former practices in the presence of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni on Vulture Peak Mountain.

Having come for the sake of hearing this Dharma discourse on the gateway of the purification of the accumulations, they attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Then the Tathāgata Śākyamuni said: "Furthermore, noble son, regarding this Dharma discourse of the Jewel-Womb..."

As the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha was speaking, forty-eight hundred thousand bodhisattvas mahāsattvas, equal in number to the sands of the river Gaṅgā, attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Bodhisattvas mahāsattvas equal in number to the atoms within a world-system of four continents attained the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika-bhūmi*).

“Equal in number to the sands of the river Gaṅgā, the bodhisattvas mahāsattvas attained the complete and perfect realization of pure knowledge regarding this Dharma discourse on the purification of the equipment for the entrance into this teaching of the gateway to meditative concentration.”
And that noble son, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahākāruṇika, by virtue of that joy and serene faith, became a youth resembling twenty years of age;
he stood following closely behind the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha.
And that noble son, King Amṛtaśuddha, together with—

Accompanied by a thousand sons, eighty thousand local kings, and ninety-two million other beings, he went forth and became a renunciant. That noble son, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahākāruṇika, applied himself with diligence to virtue, learning, meditative concentration, and gentleness. Gradually, in the presence of the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha, he studied and mastered eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma concerning the discourse on the Śrāvaka Vehicle.
He taught, recited, and mastered ninety thousand sections of the Dharma concerning the discourse on the Pratyekabuddha vehicle;

thereafter, he likewise taught, recited, and mastered one hundred thousand sections concerning the discourse on the unsurpassed Mahāyāna and the discourse on the application of mindfulness to the body,
as well as one hundred thousand sections concerning the application of mindfulness to sensation.
One hundred thousand discourses on the application of mindfulness to the mind were taught, recited, and mastered;

one hundred thousand discourses on the application of mindfulness to phenomena were taught, recited, and mastered; and one hundred thousand discourses on the elements and aggregates [were likewise taught].
A hundred thousand discourses on the aggregates of the sense bases, a hundred thousand discourses on the aggregate of abandoning the fetter of passion,
and a hundred thousand discourses on the aggregate of abandoning the fetter of hatred.

One hundred thousand discourses on the aggregate of dependent origination for the abandonment of delusion, one hundred thousand discourses on the aggregate of meditative concentrations and liberations,
and one hundred thousand [discourses].
He taught, recited, and mastered the discourse on the aggregates of the powers, the fearlessnesses, and the unique qualities of a Buddha;
indeed, he received and mastered up to one hundred thousand aggregates of the Dharma from the presence of the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha.
Then, at another time, the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, passed away into the realm of Nirvana without remainder.

And that Bodhisattva Mahākāruṇika, noble son, performed worship with various kinds of immeasurable and incalculable musical instruments, flowers, powders, garlands, perfumes, ointments, parasols, banners, flags, and jewels;
he bathed [the remains] with various fragrances and constructed a reliquary stūpa made of the seven precious gems, five yojanas in height and half a yojana in width.
